findings.title: Soviet plans were few, named, priority-ranked bets — not spreadsheets of quotas
findings.detail: The Fifth (1951-55) and Sixth (1956-abandoned-1957) Five-Year Plans and the Seven-Year Plan (1959-65) were experienced by leadership as a small number of strategic choices: which sectors got 'shock' priority (metallurgy, machine-building, defense vs. Group B consumer goods), which named projects got built (Volga-Don Canal opened 1952, the 'Great Construction Projects of Communism' hydroelectric cascade on the Volga at Kuibyshev and Stalingrad, Bratsk HES begun 1954), and which regions carried them. Gosplan generated the thousands of material balances, but the Politburo decided perhaps a dozen priorities per plan, plus one dramatic mid-plan revision when reality diverged (the Sixth FYP was scrapped outright in 1957 because its targets were infeasible — itself a ceremonial decision moment). The operating principle players should inherit: priority sectors got inputs first at near-100% of requirement; everyone else absorbed the shortfall. That single asymmetric allocation rule, not quota arithmetic, is what made planning feel like a distinct game — you chose who starves for steel.
findings.evidence: Alec Nove, An Economic History of the USSR, chs. 11-12; Eugène Zaleski, Stalinist Planning for Economic Growth; abandonment of the Sixth FYP announced Sept 1957, replaced by the Seven-Year Plan adopted at the 21st Party Congress, Feb 1959.

findings.title: The 1957 sovnarkhoz reform is the direct historical warrant for regional economic agency — and its failure mode is a mechanic
findings.detail: In May 1957 Khrushchev abolished some 140 central industrial ministries and transferred their plants to 105 regional economic councils (sovnarkhozy), the largest administrative reorganization of the Soviet economy between 1932 and 1965. The stated goal was exactly the player's complaint: decisions were being made too far from the regions. The observed pathology was 'mestnichestvo' (localism) — regions hoarded inputs, prioritized local customers, and broke cross-region supply chains, so Moscow progressively re-centralized (state committees from 1962, consolidation to 47 councils in 1962, full reversal to ministries under Kosygin in September 1965). For the game this is a ready-made structural choice: a planned economy can be administered sectorally (national levers, cross-region mismatch as the error term) or territorially (regional levers, inter-region friction as the error term). Neither dominates; each makes different information visible and different problems chronic.
findings.evidence: Law 'On Further Improving the Organization of Management of Industry and Construction,' USSR Supreme Soviet, 10 May 1957; reversal Sept 1965 plenum (Kosygin reform); Nove, Economic History of the USSR, ch. 12; Oleg Hoeffding, 'The Soviet Industrial Reorganization of 1957,' American Economic Review 49/2 (1959).

findings.title: The signature Soviet moves 1953-1962 were regional CAMPAIGNS with delayed, uncertain payoffs
findings.detail: The Virgin Lands campaign (announced Feb-Mar 1954 plenum) plowed ~30 million hectares of Kazakhstan and Western Siberia and moved ~300,000 settlers; it delivered a record 1956 harvest, then collapsed in the 1963 drought/dust storms, forcing the USSR's first large grain imports from the West. The corn campaign (1955-62) pushed maize onto climatically unsuitable regions. The MTS abolition (March 1958) sold Machine Tractor Station equipment to collective farms in one year — a stroke-of-the-pen structural reform that drained kolkhoz working capital and dented the very mechanization it meant to spread. All three share a shape: a leadership decision naming specific regions, committing labor migration and capital, with a payoff curve that ramps over 3-8 years and is modulated by weather and by whether follow-through investment happened. This is the planned economy's natural 'one decision per month' cadence: not tuning dials but launching and managing a small portfolio of named regional gambles.
findings.evidence: Feb-Mar 1954 Central Committee plenum on Virgin Lands; Martin McCauley, Khrushchev and the Development of Soviet Agriculture: The Virgin Land Programme 1953-1964; MTS liquidation law of 31 March 1958; 1963 harvest failure and Oct 1963 Canadian/US grain purchases.

findings.title: American economic agency was legislative acts, siting incentives, and procurement geography — never quantities
findings.detail: The US government shaped its economic map through one-off named acts and incentive instruments: the Federal-Aid Highway Act (signed 29 June 1956; $25B, 41,000 miles, funded by a dedicated gas-tax Highway Trust Fund), the St. Lawrence Seaway (authorized May 1954, opened 1959), and the Defense Production Act (8 Sept 1950) with its Title III loans and the rapid tax amortization certificates of 1950-53 (over $30B in certificates that let firms write off new defense plants in 5 years — the government's actual lever for WHERE aircraft, aluminum, and steel capacity got built, feeding the Sunbelt shift). Rural electrification (REA co-ops) and Interstate routing decisions had visible 10-year regional consequences: which regions industrialized, where population flowed. The player-shaped decision menu is: pass a funded infrastructure act (project-scale, rare, ceremonial in its own way — a Congressional fight), set procurement volume and placement, and offer tax/credit incentives that PRIVATE actors respond to with a lag. The market player never sets a region's output; they tilt the field and watch capital move.
findings.evidence: Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956, Pub. L. 84-627; Defense Production Act of 1950, Pub. L. 81-774; on amortization certificates and defense plant geography: Ann Markusen et al., The Rise of the Gunbelt (1991); Wiley Act (Seaway), May 1954.

findings.title: Foreign economic policy was a bidding war fought with projects, and it was legible as competition
findings.detail: The Marshall Plan (1948-52, $13.3B) involved real allocation choices — country shares hammered out through the OEEC, counterpart funds directing what each recipient rebuilt — and its Soviet answer, COMECON (founded Jan 1949, given real specialization functions from 1954-56), assigned whole industries to member states. The sharpest playable episode is the Aswan High Dam: US/UK/World Bank offered financing in December 1955, Dulles withdrew the offer on 19 July 1956, Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal on 26 July 1956, and the USSR stepped in with a ~$100M credit agreement in October 1958 and built the dam. One withdrawal decision cascaded into the Suez Crisis and a decade of Soviet influence in Egypt. The mechanic-relevant shape: development projects in third countries appear as contested opportunities; bidding costs real domestic commodities and construction capacity (the same pool the player uses at home — that scarcity coupling is the interesting part); winning buys influence and trade ties; withdrawing mid-course is itself a move with violent consequences.
findings.evidence: ECA/OEEC allocation process, 1948-52; Dulles aide-mémoire withdrawing Aswan financing, 19 July 1956 (FRUS 1955-57, vol. XV); Soviet-Egyptian agreement Oct 1958; Randall Stone, Satellites and Commissars on COMECON specialization.

findings.title: Guns-versus-butter was renegotiated at leadership moments, and the constraint was visible unrest
findings.detail: Malenkov's 'New Course' speech of 8 August 1953 promised a shift toward consumer goods (Group B) and cut retail prices; his defeat in February 1955 was argued explicitly on heavy-industry-first grounds. Khrushchev then took the butter side himself with the mass-housing decree of 31 July 1957 (the khrushchyovka prefab program — arguably the most popular thing the Soviet state ever built) and the 1957-61 'catch up with America in meat and milk' campaign (which produced the Ryazan fraud of 1959). The bill came due at Novocherkassk, 1-2 June 1962: meat and butter price rises of ~30% coinciding with factory wage-norm increases triggered a strike that was put down with ~26 dead. The design payload: the consumer/investment/military weighting the game already has should not be a free slider — reweighting happens at discrete political moments (leadership change, party congress, plan ceremony), and squeezing consumption is cheap until, region by region, it very suddenly is not.
findings.evidence: Malenkov speech to Supreme Soviet, 8 Aug 1953; Central Committee/Council of Ministers housing decree, 31 July 1957; Samuel Baron, Bloody Saturday in the Soviet Union: Novocherkassk 1962 (2001).

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Priority designation (the planned player's core verb)
mechanics_recommendations.why: This is what Soviet planning actually was at the decision level: a short ranked list of sectors/regions that eat first. It creates regional differentiation and painful tradeoffs from ONE small decision, at exactly the locked architecture's quantity-setting interface, without adding per-region quota micromanagement.
mechanics_recommendations.how: State: each region-industry complex gets an optional PriorityRank (0-3), capped at N slots total (e.g. 6), set only at plan ceremonies plus one mid-plan revision event. Formula: the existing commodity flow balance resolves in rank order — rank-1 consumers receive min(demand, supply) first, remainder cascades; unranked complexes share pro-rata. Visible output: per-region 'plan fulfillment %' and 'input satisfaction %' gauges that diverge sharply between priority and non-priority regions within 2-3 game months. Non-priority shortfall accumulates a regional discontent stock feeding the unrest system.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Named Campaigns / Great Projects with regional targets and uncertain multi-year payoff (Virgin Lands pattern)
mechanics_recommendations.why: The historically resonant Soviet decisions were regional gambles, not dial-tuning — and this is also the natural monthly-cadence decision the brief demands. It reuses the locked construction-capacity pool and named-Great-Projects concept and gives regions a story the player authored.
mechanics_recommendations.how: State: Campaign { target_regions, committed_construction_capacity, committed_labor_migration (cohort flow from donor regions), phase, base_payoff_curve }. Launching costs a large chunk of the monthly construction pool for its duration. Payoff formula: output_bonus(t) = curve(t) * weather_roll(rng.fork(b"campaign"), region) * follow_through_factor (did the player keep feeding it capacity in years 2-4?). Ramps over 36-96 game-months and CAN fail (1963 dust bowl) — failure triggers grain-import dependency, a diplomatic/hard-currency cost. Market-side twin: funded infrastructure Acts (Interstate/Seaway pattern) — a one-off legislative decision earmarking a tax stream that raises target regions' market-access/throughput modifier over ~5 years; private investment then flows there via the existing parameter interface.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Administrative structure choice for planned economies: ministerial vs sovnarkhoz
mechanics_recommendations.why: 1957/1965 proves regional decentralization is a real historical decision with real costs both ways, and it directly answers 'more player autonomy in regions' without pretending decentralization is free. It also gives planned economies a second-order strategic layer markets don't have — deepening the asymmetry.
mechanics_recommendations.how: State: enum AdminStructure { Ministerial, Sovnarkhoz } per planned country, changeable via a rare Reform decision with a 6-12 month disruption penalty to all fulfillment. Ministerial: priority slots and campaign launches are national/sectoral; error term = cross-region supply mismatch (a fixed % leakage on inter-complex flows that grows with economy size). Sovnarkhoz: priority slots are assigned per-region and regions get local mini-levers, but inter-region commodity transfers pay a 'localism' friction (regions retain X% of their own output first, X rising with regional discontent). Neither is dominant; the right choice depends on economy size and how regionally concentrated the player's campaigns are.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Regional dossier: an inspectable page per economic region, fed by petition events
mechanics_recommendations.why: Half the complaint is information, not verbs. Historically, leaders learned regional truth through reports and petitions (and famously through falsified ones — Ryazan 1959). A region the player can open, read, and be surprised by is what makes the map feel inhabited; it costs no new sim state, only surfacing what the substrate already computes.
mechanics_recommendations.how: UI: click a region in any map mode → dossier showing plan fulfillment / input satisfaction (planned) or output, prices, investment inflow (market), power balance vs. its named grid, commodity shortfalls, cohort trends and migration, living standard, discontent, active campaigns/projects touching it. Sim: a monthly 'reports' system emits 2-4 prioritized regional notices (worst fulfillment gap, grid throttling, discontent threshold crossed, campaign milestone) into an inbox — each deep-links to the dossier and, where applicable, offers the relevant decision (add priority slot, divert construction, release reserves). Planned-economy flavor: report accuracy degrades with discontent/pressure (padding), so a region can lie until an inspection event reveals it.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Contested foreign development projects (Aswan pattern)
mechanics_recommendations.why: It fuses pillar 4 with pillars 2 and 3, and its cost side couples to the domestic economy — bidding for Aswan spends the same construction capacity and commodities the player wants at home, which is the actual Cold War tradeoff and makes the domestic economy matter geopolitically.
mechanics_recommendations.how: State: a scripted+procedural stream of ProjectOpportunity { host_country, cost (construction capacity + specific commodities over N months), influence_payoff, trade_tie }. Both superpowers may bid; host accepts on an alignment+generosity score. Winner pays the flow cost from its domestic pools (visible as a drag in the econ panel) and gains influence, a trade route, and a named completed project on the map. Withdrawing mid-project (the Dulles move) refunds remaining cost but fires a hostility/realignment event chain. 5-10 such opportunities per decade keeps it at decision cadence, not management.

pitfalls: Do not scale the plan interface to the region count. With ~250 regions the deadly temptation is 250 quota rows. Historically the center made perhaps a dozen priority calls and launched one or two campaigns a year; if the redesign asks the player for more decisions than the Politburo actually made, it becomes the spreadsheet the architecture was designed to avoid. Keep verbs scarce (priority slots capped, campaigns expensive) and let information, not decisions, be the thing that scales per-region.

Do not let the market side become planning with different labels. The US never set regional quantities; its agency was rare funded Acts, tax/amortization incentives, and procurement placement, with private capital responding on a lag. If the market player can directly choose a region's output or industry mix, the asymmetry thesis — the game's stated pillar — is dead. The market player's regional feeling should come from watching incentives take, not from allocation.

Do not make campaigns deterministic buttons. Virgin Lands was a triumph in 1956 and a catastrophe in 1963; if a campaign's payoff is a known curve, it is just a purchase. Weather/variance from SimRng (deterministic per seed, unknown to the player) plus a follow-through requirement is what makes launching one feel like a decision rather than a transaction.

Do not gate regional information behind regional control. The sovnarkhoz mechanic could tempt a design where you only see regions you administer regionally. Historically the center always had (imperfect, sometimes falsified) regional reporting under both structures. Inspectability should be universal from day one; what the admin-structure choice changes is the error term and lever placement, not the map's legibility.
analysts.first_hour_test: A new USSR player boots January 1950 and opens the economy. They SEE a plan ceremony screen (the game is paused): six priority slots, two filled by scenario defaults (Donbass coal, Urals metallurgy), a list of three launchable named projects (Volga-Don Canal, Kuibyshev HES, a Kazakhstan land-development study), and behind it a region map colored by input-satisfaction, where clicking Donbass opens a dossier — fulfillment 94%, grid strained, discontent low, a cohort chart. Their first DECISION is spending the remaining priority slots and committing this year's construction capacity to one named project, knowing non-priority regions will visibly starve for inputs. It feels like playing rather than watching because within two or three game-months the map answers back: priority regions' gauges climb, a petition arrives from an unranked region whose satisfaction fell to 60%, and the Korean War (June 1950) forces the question of whether to burn a mid-plan revision to swing a slot to military industry. The USA player's mirror: no quantity screen exists — they see regional prices, investment inflow, and idle capacity; their first decision is placing the Korean rearmament procurement and offering rapid-amortization certificates to two regions, then watching over months whether private capacity actually shows up where they tilted the field. Same map, same dossiers, opposite verbs — which is the pillar working as stated."

analysts.analyst: asymmetric-agency (planned-vs-market interface design; W&R, Capitalism Lab, Kremlingames, Kanban/FCM lens)

findings.title: The asymmetry must live in the DECISION STREAM, not just the lever set — planner commands, market player responds to proposals
findings.detail: The v1 asymmetry (quota rows vs lever rows) is real but both are 'adjust numbers in a panel', which is why it feels like watching. The deeper asymmetry from the references: in Workers & Resources YOU are the demand — nothing happens unless the state orders it — while in Capitalism Lab the state only tilts the field and autonomous firms generate all the activity; the player's macro levers (rates, taxes, spending) work by changing what firms choose to do. Food Chain Magnate makes the same point in board form: demand literally does not exist until an actor creates it with marketing. Translate this into interface grammar: the planned player initiates (issues targets, flags priorities, directs labor — the sim executes and fails), while the market player disposes (firms and regions generate proposals, contract bids, grant requests, crisis events into an inbox; the player accepts, declines, or reprices). Both get roughly the same decisions-per-month, but one is authoring the economy and the other is refereeing it. That inversion is the first-hour difference the pillar demands, and neither side ever sees the other's UI surfaces.
findings.evidence: W&R realistic mode: all construction requires state-provided materials via construction offices (steamcommunity.com/app/784150 discussions; wiki.hoodedhorse.com W&R roadmap). Capitalism Lab macro sim: player-set rates/taxes act through firm borrowing/investment decisions, never through commands (capitalismlab.com/enhanced-macroeconomic-simulation, /learn-macroeconomics). Food Chain Magnate demand-creation logic (boardgamegeek.com/boardgame/175914). Matches locked principle 7 in docs/research/economy-mechanics.md.

findings.title: Planned agency = scarce priority flags plus batched ceremonies; the historical Soviet priority system is the mechanic, not flavor
findings.detail: The actual Gosplan mechanism that made an unsolvable allocation problem playable was priority: a short list of sectors/projects that got first claim on materials, power, rail, and labor, with everything else absorbing the residual shortage. This is a perfect game verb because it is inherently scarce, zero-sum, and regional: give the planned player 3-5 priority flags to place on named regions/complexes at Plan ceremonies, and between ceremonies only a thin set of interrupt verbs — move one flag (cooldown), direct a labor draft from region A to region B (consent/SoL cost, arrives over weeks), order an audit, or call a 'storming' surge (end-of-quarter output spike that eats quality/depreciation, the historical shturmovshchina). Prioritized regions get a power-throttle floor and first position in the commodity balance resolution order; unprioritized regions eat the cascade. This keeps planned cadence at the locked one-big-decision-per-month scale while making every shortage traceable to a placement the player chose — agency through scarcity of attention, which Kanban proves is fun: its whole game is scarce action slots inside a factory bureaucracy plus a periodic scored performance review against announced targets.
findings.evidence: Soviet priority planning (Zaleski, 'Stalinist Planning for Economic Growth'; standard in the planned-economy literature). Kanban's audit/scored-review and scarce-slot structure (boardgamegeek.com/boardgame/284378, medium.com/theuglymonster Kanban EV review). Fits research principle 10 (attention is the scaled resource) and the existing FYP-ceremony architecture in docs/design/systems/planning-interfaces.md.

findings.title: Market agency = a contract book and one incentive zone; the market player touches regions by dangling money, never by placing things
findings.detail: The market player's regional verb set: (1) award procurement contracts to NAMED regional complexes — when the bomber program opens, Boeing/Seattle and Convair/Fort Worth both bid, and choosing is a real decision with price, delivery, and regional-politics consequences; (2) designate one active regional incentive zone (tax abatement / accelerated depreciation) that biases where autonomous private investment lands, computed from regional ROI (SoL, power factor, labor pool, tax); (3) countercyclical parameter moves when the business-cycle state machine turns (see failure asymmetry). Critically, contracts stay parameter-shaped: the player sets a price and a quantity ceiling, the firm decides fulfillment rate — the moment a contract lets the market player command quantities, the thesis collapses into Supreme Ruler's 'communism = capitalism with modifiers' dead end. Private investment visibly building things in regions the player merely tilted is also the market side's best spectacle: the player should regularly see 'a new complex opened in Region X' that they influenced but did not order.
findings.evidence: Capitalism Lab CES DLC: macro policy acts on firm behavior, recessions emerge from rate/inflation dynamics (capitalismlab.com/ces-dlc, /new-features/inflation). Historical: 1950s US defense procurement competitions (B-47/B-52 programs) as named-complex contract awards. Anti-pattern warning from research readup principle 7 (Supreme Ruler).

findings.title: Failure-mode asymmetry: the planner's map lies until audited; the market's map is honest but its levers lag
findings.detail: Extend the existing country-level misreporting to per-region reported-vs-actual drift (drift grows with the gap between quota and actual, capped ~15%), and make the planned player's region cards and plan-fulfillment map mode show REPORTED. The audit verb (an inspection trip) resets one region's reported to actual at a stability cost with a cooldown — so the planner's core loop is epistemic: read proxy tells (queue index, black-market share, letters/complaint events), decide which region is lying, spend a scarce action to find out, then repair with a priority flag or labor draft. Shortage cascades propagate through the chain (steel region starves machine region starves everything) and the cascade is only visible where you have audited. The market player instead gets Ostalgie/Capitalism-Lab-style honest leading indicators per region — unemployment, price index, business confidence — and a 4-state business cycle (expansion/peak/recession/trough driven by the inflation-rate gap): they can see the recession coming a year out but rate cuts take months to bite and can never command a region back to health, plus capital-flight/strike events as the acute form. Symmetric information ARCHITECTURE (both get a rich regional ledger card, answering the player complaint directly), asymmetric information TRUTHFULNESS and asymmetric lever latency.
findings.evidence: Kremlingames titles (Crisis in the Kremlin, Ostalgie) show sector-spending + shortage + distorted-statistics loops carry a whole game, and their 'economy feels broken' reviews show the failure mode when deception lacks tells (store.steampowered.com/app/599750, steamshovelers.cool review). Existing misreporting mechanic in docs/design/systems/planning-interfaces.md (open question 'audits' answered: yes, regionally). Research principle 10: planner dashboard shows plan data, not truth.

findings.title: Tedium parity is a measurable budget: batch the planner, event-drive the market player, and never descend below region resolution
findings.detail: The two classic collapses: planned becomes strictly more clicks (W&R realistic mode is beloved but its own community describes 5-6 hours of watching vehicles to build a first town — the tedium cliff of literal logistics), and market becomes strictly less interactive (set rates once, watch line go up — Capitalism Lab's macro layer alone is a spectator mode without the business layer under it). The fix is a decision budget: target roughly 2-4 meaningful economy decisions per game-month for BOTH systems, sourced differently. Planned: ceremony every plan period + ~1 interrupt verb (flag move, audit, labor draft) per month, each heavy. Market: ~1-2 inbox proposals per month (contract bids, grant requests, bailout asks) + occasional rate-meeting moments when indicators cross thresholds, each light but consequential. Both are pause-friendly and neither requires per-tick attention. All verbs on both sides address regions/complexes as the atomic unit — never provinces, never individual buildings — preserving the locked one-construction-decision-per-month cadence and the ~250-region resolution.
findings.evidence: W&R realistic-mode tedium reports (steamcommunity.com/app/784150 realistic-mode threads); The Political Machine's per-state polling map + public-promise structure as the model for cheap regional legibility with sparse decisions; research principle 10 (aggregate to ~one construction decision per month, chunky beats sliders).

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Regional Ledger Card + system-specific map modes (shared substrate, asymmetric truth)
mechanics_recommendations.why: Directly answers the player complaint — regions become inspectable places — while carrying the pillar: same card skeleton, different numbers and different trustworthiness per system. Cheap to build on data that already exists (regions, grids, cohorts, balances).
mechanics_recommendations.how: Click any region → card: population/labor cohorts, power factor, named complexes, food status, SoL, plus a system block. Planned block: per-region quota vs REPORTED fulfillment %, queue index, black-market index, last-audit date; new state `RegionEconReport { actual: FixedPoint, reported: FixedPoint, last_audit: SimDate }` with monthly drift `reported += clamp(k*(quota_expectation - actual), 0, cap)` capped at +15% over actual, keyed in a BTreeMap<RegionId,_>. Market block: TRUE regional output, unemployment %, price index, business confidence. Two new map modes: 'plan fulfillment' (tints by reported %, planned countries only) and 'economic climate' (tints by true growth/unemployment, market only). The map mode itself differs by system — the first thing a new player sees is already asymmetric.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Priority Flags + interrupt verbs (the planned agency package)
mechanics_recommendations.why: Gives the Gosplan player verbs the market player never sees, generates the hidden-shortage-cascade failure mode mechanically instead of scripting it, and stays inside the one-decision-per-month budget because flags are scarce and moves are cooldown-gated.
mechanics_recommendations.how: State: `PriorityFlags: BTreeSet<RegionId>` with budget 3 (grows with a later institution). Effects in the monthly economy resolve: flagged regions get power-throttle floor 1.0, first claim in commodity/chain shortfall allocation (resolve order: flagged regions in RegionId order, then unflagged), and +labor-inflow weighting. Commands (planned-only, validated like SetPlannedAllocation): `MoveFlag { from, to }` (1/quarter), `AuditRegion { region }` (sets reported=actual, stability −X, 3-month cooldown per region), `LaborDraft { from, to, thousands }` (cohort transfer over N weeks, consent/SoL cost in source region), `StormingSurge { region }` (output ×1.2 for one month, depreciation ×3 that month). Flags are set/reset wholesale at the FYP ceremony; interrupts are the between-ceremony game.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Contract Book + Incentive Zone (the market agency package)
mechanics_recommendations.why: Gives the market player an initiative stream without letting them command quantities: firms propose, the player disposes. Named regional complexes bidding on procurement makes market regions memorable the same way named Great Projects do for the planner.
mechanics_recommendations.how: A deterministic proposal generator (fork `rng.fork(b"contracts")`, monthly, seeded from procurement level + military demand + which complexes exist) emits 1-2 inbox items: `ContractBid { complex_a, complex_b, price_a, price_b, delivery }` (award to one; the winning region gains investment inflow and the military stockpile gains scheduled deliveries — quantity CEILING and price, firm chooses fulfillment rate from profitability), `GrantRequest`, and during recessions `BailoutAsk`. One `IncentiveZone { region }` active at a time (market-only command): multiplies that region's ROI term in the private-investment allocator `invest_share_r = ROI_r / Σ ROI` where `ROI_r = f(SoL_r, power_r, labor_r, tax) × zone_bonus`. Business-cycle state machine: `enum Cycle { Expansion, Peak, Recession, Trough }`, transitions monthly from smoothed(inflation − interest) and confidence; Recession cuts private investment and consumer demand, spikes unemployment, and is when rate/tax moves matter most (lag: policy effects phase in over 3-6 months via a small ring buffer).

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Diegetic tells for the lying map (planned) and leading indicators (market)
mechanics_recommendations.why: Region-level misreporting reads as a bug, not a theme, unless the player can FEEL the lie without seeing truth — the Kremlingames 'economy is broken' reviews are the cautionary tale. Symmetrically, the market's honest data is only an advantage if it actually leads events.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Planned: queue index and black-market index per region are computed from ACTUAL (consumer shortfall vs quota) but always shown truthfully — they are the observable shadow of the lie; monthly flavor events ('Letter from Sverdlovsk: meat has not been seen since March') fire when reported−actual exceeds a threshold, drawn deterministically. Market: confidence and unemployment indicators are computed from the cycle state machine one transition AHEAD (peak indicators degrade before Recession fires), so a player who reads region cards gets a genuine 2-3 month warning. Both are pure presentation over sim state already computed — no new sim coupling.

pitfalls: Decision-count asymmetry becomes system imbalance: if the planned side needs 6 clicks/month and the market side 1, planned is strictly more tedious and everyone plays USA. Budget ~2-4 meaningful decisions/month for both and playtest against that number explicitly; the market inbox exists precisely to keep the market player's count up.

Misreporting without tells reads as a broken game, not a deceptive apparatus — Crisis in the Kremlin's reception shows players call an opaque planned economy 'buggy'. Every lie needs an honest shadow (queues, black-market index, complaint events) so discovering fraud feels like detective work, not like the sim ignoring inputs.

Priority flags that aren't scarce collapse the planned game: if the player can flag everything (or move flags freely), shortage cascades never bite and planning becomes a solved checkbox. Keep the flag budget small, moves cooldown-gated, and make the ceremony the only wholesale reset.

Contracts that set quantities turn the market player into a second Gosplan — Supreme Ruler's 'capitalism with modifiers' failure. Contracts fix price and ceiling only; if a firm under-delivers because the price was too low, that IS the market game working.

Workers & Resources' tedium cliff: the moment any verb addresses a province or an individual building instead of a region/complex, the 4,594-province map makes it micromanagement hell. All new verbs must be region-or-coarser; W&R's realistic mode proves literal logistics is a different (city-builder) game, not this one.

Building the agency layer before the region cards: verbs without legibility recreate the current complaint in reverse (things to do, still nowhere to look). Ship the Regional Ledger Card and the two asymmetric map modes FIRST — inspection is the prerequisite for every verb above being a decision rather than a guess.
analysts.first_hour_test: Boot as USSR, January 1950, press E. The economy panel now opens alongside a 'plan fulfillment' map mode: every region tinted by reported fulfillment, three gold priority flags sitting on Donbass, the Urals, and Moscow — placed by the scenario, visibly yours to move. Click the Donbass card: coal 104% of quota (reported), but the queue index is climbing and the black-market index just ticked up — the card is telling you two stories and they disagree. The first economic DECISION, inside the first hour: either spend your audit on Donbass (and eat the stability cost) to learn the real number, or trust the report and move a priority flag east to the machine-building regions the next Plan needs. Either way you have placed a scarce chip against a map you know is partially lying to you — that is playing, not watching, because the sim's output is now a puzzle your verbs act on. Boot as USA instead: the same E key opens an honest 'economic climate' map — true unemployment and growth per region — and an inbox holds one item: two named aircraft complexes bidding on the new bomber contract, Seattle cheaper, Fort Worth in a region whose card shows unemployment rising. Award it, watch private investment start flowing to the winner on its own, and note the inflation indicator creeping as procurement rises — the rate decision you will face in three months is already visible. Same substrate, same hour, two different games: the Soviet player interrogates a beautiful lie and commands; the American player reads true instruments and tilts.

findings.title: The load-bearing loop is one universal verb that every problem routes into
findings.detail: Victoria 3's economy is a game rather than a dashboard because nearly every observed problem resolves into the same verb: queue a building in a state. High prices? Build supply. Unemployment or radicals? Build jobs. Low SoL? Build the goods pops want. This universality is what reviewers mean by 'one enormous feedback loop, where the tiniest tweak... can have enormous economic and social ramifications' — the player always knows what the move IS, and construction's slow weekly progress supplies commitment and anticipation. The failure mode is equally instructive: because the verb is universal and cheap to invoke, 'end game consists of nonstop construction of factories to meet increasing demand' and the community literally petitioned to end the construction-queue mechanic. UGS should keep the universality (every regional problem should route to a legible response) but throttle invocation frequency: the locked ~one-construction-decision-per-month cadence is precisely the fix for Vic3's queue-feeding treadmill, provided that single decision is presented as a rich choice among named regional alternatives rather than a rubber stamp.
findings.evidence: Kotaku review (kotaku.com/victoria-3-review-...): 'one enormous feedback loop'; Paradox forum 'Petition to end the construction queue mechanic' (forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/petition-to-end-the-construction-queue-mechanic.1594102); Steam discussions on endgame as nonstop queue-feeding.

findings.title: A state feels like a place when it answers three questions at a glance: what's here, who's here, what binds it
findings.detail: Vic3's state view works because a state has identity (resource potentials and arable land make Silesia mean coal and Bengal mean jute), inhabitants (pops with professions, employment bars filling as a building staffs up, SoL per pop), and constraints (market access %, infrastructure, arable-land caps, qualification shortages). The employment bar is quietly the best trick: a new building is not an instant stat bump but an unfolding story of people moving into jobs over months — the sim made visible at human scale. Market access is the cautionary half of the lesson: a per-state derived quantity whose failure produces 'death spirals' players can't attribute (local prices diverging from national prices in opaque ways). For UGS the region dossier must lead with identity (named complexes, grid membership, cohort structure) and must COMPUTE the binding constraint rather than leaving the player to infer it — Vic3 only gestures at this with shortage icons, and its most-cursed bugs are exactly where the constraint chain became illegible.
findings.evidence: Victoria 3 wiki Building/Market pages (vic3.paradoxwikis.com/Building, /Market); StrateGGames market-access guide on the state 'death spiral' (old.strateggames.com/a/market-access-guide-for-victoria-3/); Dev Diary #13 on SoL tiers (forum.paradoxplaza.com/.../victoria-3-dev-diary-13-standard-of-living.1489327).

findings.title: Prices-with-drill-down turn sim state into a to-do list — until the causal chain lies
findings.detail: The market panel is Vic3's agenda-setting device: a sorted list of goods by price deviation is effectively a ranked list of profitable player actions, and each good drills down to buy/sell orders, then to the specific buildings and states behind them. This click-through chain from aggregate symptom to regional cause is what makes inspection feel like detective work rather than reading a report. It breaks exactly where the sim cheats: goods created ex nihilo to fill shortages and unsold goods 'sold to the void', the ±75% price clamp making permanent shortage a viable strategy, and local/national price desync — players hit a wall where the drill-down no longer explains the number, and the game reverts to wiki homework ('The Fundamentally Broken Economics of Victoria 3'). Lesson for UGS: every aggregate on the econ panel (commodity balance, industry output, power) must decompose into per-region rows that decompose into named complexes, and the sim must never fabricate quantities the inspector can't account for. The one licensed exception is the planner's falsified fulfillment reports — but there the deception is the mechanic, and it must be discoverable as deception (audits, espionage cross-checks), not merely wrong.
findings.evidence: Paradox forum thread 'The Fundamentally Broken Economics of Victoria 3' (forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/the-fundamentally-broken-economics-of-victoria-3.1733170); games.gg market guides on the +75% clamp and shortage throughput spiral; Steam 'Economic Death Spiral' discussions.

findings.title: Macro-micro tedium is a decision-frequency bug: identical per-state decisions scale linearly with empire size
findings.detail: Vic3's late-game collapse into chore is well documented: production-method 'whack-a-mole' re-toggled per building per state after every tech, queue-feeding across 50+ states, and performance so poor 'many players can't effectively play past 1890'. The root cause is architectural: the game exposes per-state toggles for what are really national policy decisions (electrify the steel industry), so decision count grows with states owned while decision VARIETY stays flat. UGS at ~250 regions would be 5x worse if it copied the shape. The fix the locked architecture already implies: modernization and technique changes are national/plan-level step changes that roll out across regions on their own schedule; the player's per-region attention is reserved for the scarce monthly allocation and for exceptions the sim surfaces (a complex missing quota, a grid browning out). Vic3's own 1.5-era answer — splitting construction into a government queue plus an autonomous private queue — half-worked at best: players report the private AI 'makes awful decisions' and that they lost control without gaining a different game, which is a direct warning for UGS's market interface.
findings.evidence: Paradox forum 'The production micromanagement kills me' (forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/...1556414); Steam late-game/perf threads; Dev Diary #71 Autonomous Investment (paradoxinteractive.com/games/victoria-3/news/dev-diary-71-autonomous-investment-in-1-2) and Steam threads on private construction dissatisfaction.

findings.title: The asymmetry warning: Vic3's 'laissez-faire = same game minus control' is the exact trap UGS's market interface must dodge
findings.detail: Vic3 tried to make interventionism-vs-laissez-faire matter by reallocating construction points between government and private queues, with an investment-pool AI building on pops' behalf. The result is the community's least-loved system: the private AI builds unprofitable or strategically absurd things, the player experiences it as the same building game played worse by someone else, and mods exist solely to re-centralize control. This proves that 'market economy = planned economy with an AI middleman' is as dead an end as 'communism = capitalism with modifiers'. For UGS's asymmetry thesis to survive contact with the player, the market side must be a genuinely different and genuinely good game: the player's verbs are parameters (rates, tax credits, procurement contracts, zoning) and the payoff is a LEGIBLE investment response — a per-region investment-climate readout that shows why capital flowed where it did, so parameter-setting feels like steering a river rather than begging an AI. Conversely the planner keeps the Vic3-style direct allocation verb, at monthly cadence, which is where that verb is historically and mechanically honest.
findings.evidence: Steam Workshop 'Grey's Smarter Private Construction' and 'Private Sector Construction' mods (existence of re-centralizing mods is the evidence); Steam 'Private Construction allocation' discussions; Wargamer 'Victoria 3's top mods turn it back into a spreadsheet simulator' (wargamer.com/victoria-3/spreadsheet-mods).

findings.title: A panel without a verb is still a dashboard — Vic3 stays alive only where inspection feeds action within one click
findings.detail: Destructoid's line — 'it may always look like it's breathing, but rarely is Victoria 3 ever truly alive' — lands where the game shows numbers with no adjacent move. What keeps the good 90% of Vic3 alive is that map modes and panels are decision surfaces: the SoL map mode implies where to build, the market panel implies what to build, the state view's expand button is right next to the employment bar it affects. The player's complaint about UGS ('watching a simulation... nowhere to look, nothing to do') is precisely a missing-verb-adjacency problem: regions are computed but the region is not a screen, and the screen that exists (country stats) has three levers unmoored from any place. Every element of the coming region dossier should pass the test 'what does the player DO from here?' — a bottleneck line links to the construction proposal that relieves it; a commodity deficit row links to the priority list or procurement contract; an SoL warning links to the consumer-goods quota. Where the honest answer is 'nothing yet', the element should either surface an event choice or be cut.
findings.evidence: Destructoid review (destructoid.com/reviews/review-victoria-3-pc-paradox-interactive-strategy/); Kotaku review; TheGamer preview on UI drawing eyes to pertinent, actionable information.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Region Dossier with a computed binding-constraint line
mechanics_recommendations.why: Makes regions legible places (the player's explicit ask) by stealing Vic3's state-view strengths — identity, inhabitants, constraint — while fixing its weakness: Vic3 makes the player infer the bottleneck; UGS should state it, because argmin is already how the sim throttles output.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Click any region (map or list) → panel with: header (name, cohorts rural/urban/educated, urbanization %, SoL sparkline over 24 months); named industrial complexes with capacity, employment, utilization %; grid membership with generation/demand and throttle %; commodity in/out flow rows. One highlighted line per complex: utilization = min(labor_avail, power_avail, input_avail, capital) with the argmin named and quantified — 'Donbas Steel: 82% — limited by electricity (−18%)'. Each constraint links to the verb that relieves it (construction proposal, priority list, quota). Planner variant renders REPORTED figures from fulfillment reports; a divergence stat per region (hidden, driven by pressure-to-falsify) corrupts them, discoverable via audits/espionage. State needed: per-region complex records (already implied by regionalizing the industry scalar), per-region monthly report snapshot, falsification scalar.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Monthly construction council: sim-drafted regional proposals, player disposes
mechanics_recommendations.why: This is Vic3's core verb — place capacity in a place — delivered at the locked one-decision-per-month cadence, killing the queue-feeding treadmill while keeping the universal-verb property. It also gives the planner interface its ceremonial texture: Gosplan proposes, the player decides.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Construction capacity pool accrues points; each new_month, the sim drafts 3–5 candidate projects (deterministic scoring over regional bottlenecks: worst power deficit, largest idle labor reserve, biggest input gap, plus any queued Great Project stage) each with region, cost, build time, and predicted effect ('+120 MW to Donbas grid, unthrottles steel ~15%'). Player approves one (or reorders a small standing queue of 2–3), can reject all and pick manually from the region dossier's build tab for the same cost. Great Projects occupy multiple months of the pool and carry overrun-risk events. Market variant: the player never picks projects; the same proposal engine runs as private investment weighted by regional profit and the player's parameter verbs — tax credits, procurement contracts, development zones targeted at named regions — with a monthly 'where capital went and why' digest so steering is visible. State: proposal list resource, per-region project-in-progress records, parameter modifiers per region.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Bottleneck map modes plus a regional econ inbox
mechanics_recommendations.why: Vic3 stays playable because map modes and price lists are ranked to-do lists; UGS currently surfaces almost nothing regional, so the sim's drama (throttled grids, missed quotas, labor exhaustion) happens invisibly. Attention routing is the cheapest possible agency multiplier on systems already implemented.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Map modes: power balance (already exists — extend with throttle overlay), labor reserve (rural cohort minus subsistence need = urbanizable surplus), SoL/consumer deprivation, and plan fulfillment % (planner) / profit rate (market). Each mode's legend states the implied action. Econ inbox: deterministic monthly event feed of region-scoped items — 'Kuzbass complex reports 78% of quota', 'Baku grid throttling refineries', 'Ukraine grain quota met; livestock slaughter reported' — each with jump-to-region and, where meaningful, a 2–3 option response (accept report / order audit; raise quota / lower quota; reallocate priority). Cap at ~3–5 items/month via severity ranking so it curates rather than spams. State: event queue keyed by (month, region, kind), thresholds in a tuning module.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Commodity ledger with full regional drill-down and planner priority lists
mechanics_recommendations.why: Vic3's good→orders→buildings click-chain is what makes inspection feel like investigation, and its ex-nihilo cheats are what break trust. UGS already computes regional flow balances; exposing the decomposition is mostly UI, and the planner's shortage-incidence ordering is a real quantities-verb that markets answer with prices — the asymmetry made visible in one screen.
mechanics_recommendations.how: National commodity row (already shown) expands to per-region producer/consumer rows; each row links to the region dossier and the specific complex. On deficit, show incidence: which consumers got shorted, in what order. Planner: that order is a player-editable priority list per commodity (military > heavy industry > consumer, reorderable — deterministic tie-break by region id), so 'who starves first' is a decision, historically the decision. Market: incidence falls out of price — highest-cost marginal buyers drop first, shown as which firms/households curtailed, feeding unemployment and the influence war. Never fabricate supply to close a gap; the ledger must sum. State: per-commodity priority Vec<ConsumerClass> for planned countries; curtailment records per region-month for the drill-down.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Employment ramp and visible progress on everything slow
mechanics_recommendations.why: Vic3's employment bar and construction progress turn stat changes into unfolding stories — the anticipation engine that makes 'line go up' emotionally load-bearing. UGS's monthly cadence makes slow visible progress even more important: between decisions, the player needs things to WATCH that they caused.
mechanics_recommendations.how: New complexes and Great Projects staff up over months from the regional labor reserve (migration gated by housing per the locked architecture), shown as a filling bar in the dossier plus a projected full-capacity date. Construction shows monthly progress with named stages for Great Projects ('excavation → lock construction → flooding' for Volga-Don) and a completion moment (newsreel-style toast, influence payout). Quota fulfillment renders as month-by-month bars against plan targets so a Five-Year Plan is a wall chart the player rereads. State: per-complex staffing fraction, per-project stage index — trivial additions to records the other mechanics already require.

pitfalls: Do not ship per-region build queues at 250 regions — that is Vic3's 50-state whack-a-mole times five. All volume flows through the single monthly decision plus national-level step-change modernization; per-region toggles for what are really national policies (electrification, mechanization) are the tedium bug, not depth.

Do not implement the market interface as 'the planner's game played by a dumb AI'. Vic3's private-construction pool is its least-loved system precisely because players lost control without gaining a different game (re-centralizing mods are the tombstone). Market agency must come from parameters with visible, attributable regional response — if the player cannot see why capital moved, the western half of the asymmetry thesis dies.

No panel without a verb. Every region-dossier element must link to an action (proposal, priority list, quota, contract) or surface a choice; a read-only stats screen reproduces the exact 'watching a simulation' complaint that motivated this work.

Never fabricate quantities the inspector cannot account for. Vic3's ex-nihilo goods, void sales, and ±75% price clamps are where its drill-down lies and player trust collapses into wiki homework. The one sanctioned lie is the planner's falsified fulfillment reports — and that lie must be a discoverable mechanic (audits, espionage cross-checks, divergence between reported and observed), not silent wrongness.

Watch the inbox volume. An event feed that scales with region count becomes HoI4-notification spam; severity-rank and cap it (~3–5 regional items per month) so it curates attention rather than demanding it.
analysts.first_hour_test: A new USSR player opens the economy panel in January 1950. They SEE: the national plan overview (quota permilles, this month's fulfillment bars) and a map in plan-fulfillment mode where Donbas, the Urals, and Kuzbass glow as named places with numbers. They click Donbas: the dossier shows the coal and steel complexes with employment bars, the Donbas grid at 94% of demand, an SoL sparkline, and one highlighted line — 'Donbas Steel: 82% — limited by electricity (−18%)'. At the month boundary the game pulses paused: Gosplan presents three proposals — a thermal power station on the Donbas grid, a tractor plant in the Urals, housing in Moscow — each with cost, timeline, and predicted effect. The player picks the power station BECAUSE THEY SAW THE BOTTLENECK, then reorders the coal priority list so steel eats before households (and notes the SoL warning that creates). Their first economic decision is thus a diagnosis they made themselves, spent against a scarce monthly budget, with a progress bar to watch and a February fulfillment report that will confirm or betray them — and 'betray' is live, because the report is Donbas's word, not ground truth. It feels like playing because the loop is inspect place → identify constraint → commit scarce increment → watch consequences ramp, not read national aggregates while three unmoored levers idle. The USA mirror: the player sees prices and profit rates instead of quotas, targets an investment tax credit at the Gulf Coast refining region, and the monthly digest shows private capital breaking ground there and explains why — steering, not commanding, and visibly working.

analysts.analyst: ui-information-design (region legibility, inspectors, map modes, drill-down)

findings.title: The region inspector must be a one-page dossier that prints causes inline — never a tooltip archaeology dig
findings.detail: Victoria 3 is the genre's canonical failure and it is an information-ARCHITECTURE failure, not a data failure: the data exists but lives under nested hover-tooltips, multi-window drill-downs, and 'current situation' dropdowns, so players cannot answer 'why is this state poor' without wiki homework. The community's response is literally a mod category ('More Informative Panel Tooltips'). This game already solved the identical problem for war: the battle inspector prints the top modifiers per side inline, then auto-diagnoses with one generated sentence ('You are losing primarily because of the mountain defense'). The region inspector should be the same form: a FIXED single-page teletype dossier with an identity header (name, country, population + trend, region character line like 'COAL / HEAVY INDUSTRY'), four stat blocks (PEOPLE, POWER, PRODUCTION, FOOD), and a footer that names the binding constraint plus one templated assessment sentence ('URALS OUTPUT LIMITED BY POWER: GENERATION COVERS 82% OF DEMAND'). Fixed layout matters: the player learns to read it in one game-month and thereafter scans it in two seconds — the NATO-counter lesson from the war research applied to economics. Everything on the page is flat text; nothing requires a second hover to understand.
findings.evidence: docs/research/war-legibility.md principles 3-4 and the shipped battle inspector (same complaint, same fix, already validated in this codebase); Vic3 tooltip-burial criticism per [Vic3 wiki UI page](https://vic3.paradoxwikis.com/User_interface) and the [More Informative Panel Tooltips mod thread](https://forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/mod-more-informative-panel-tooltips.1620359/); [Paradox Dev Diary #74 UX Improvements](https://www.paradoxinteractive.com/games/victoria-3/news/dev-diary-74-ux-improvements) is Paradox itself conceding the drill-down problem post-release.

findings.title: Bottleneck-first display: at 250 regions the unit of information is the binding constraint, not the flow table
findings.detail: Cities: Skylines' traffic deep-dive states the principle exactly: the overlay was redesigned to paint ONLY the bottleneck red because inexperienced players could not find the problem when everything was colored. Frostpunk compresses a whole society into two bars (hope/discontent) and pushes detail behind demand. At 250 regions no player will read 250 flow tables — but the sim already knows, for every region, which single factor is currently limiting output (power_factor, labor availability, input commodity ratio, plan allocation, later transport). Compute argmin per region monthly and make that one word the region's public status: 'POWER-LIMITED', 'LABOR-SHORT', 'COAL-STARVED', 'UNCONSTRAINED'. This converts the region layer from a data lake into a triage list, which is precisely the cognitive shape of the locked cadence: one construction decision per game-month means the player's real question is 'where does this month's shovel go', and constraint-first display answers it directly.
findings.evidence: [Game Design Deep Dive: Traffic systems in Cities: Skylines](https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/game-design-deep-dive-traffic-systems-in-i-cities-skylines-i-) (bottleneck-painting rationale); [Cities: Skylines Dev Diary 9: Info Views](https://forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/cities-skylines-dev-diary-9-info-views.833752/); docs/research/economy-mechanics.md principle 2 (the binding constraint is DESIGNED to migrate across the campaign — so the UI's job is to show where it currently sits); power_factor already computed in crates/ugs-sim per docs/design/systems/resources-and-grids.md.

findings.title: Map modes earn their place only when paired with a verb; four economic modes, not one per commodity
findings.detail: Cities: Skylines ships 36 info views because it is a sandbox builder where every overlay maps to a placeable object; a grand strategy game that copied that count would drown the player (and Vic3's map-mode pile is already criticized as underused). The test for a mode: 'what decision does a player make while looking at it?' Four pass: (1) POWER — exists today; verb: build generation / interconnect. (2) BOTTLENECK — categorical color by constraint type, intensity by severity; verb: aim the monthly construction allocation. (3) FOOD SECURITY — production vs demand ratio with procurement-quota risk shading; verb: adjust quota / procurement before the famine, the political-catastrophe early-warning radar. (4) LIVING STANDARDS (relative SoL vs the other bloc) — the influence-war battleground from the cross-bloc scoreboard; verb: consumer-goods allocation / jamming / influence ops. Eight per-commodity map modes fail the test — a coal map with no coal verb is decoration. Commodity detail belongs in the dossier and ledger, not on the map.
findings.evidence: [Cities: Skylines Info views wiki](https://skylines.paradoxwikis.com/Info_views) (36 views — the anti-pattern at grand-strategy scale); [Victoria 3 Map modes wiki](https://vic3.paradoxwikis.com/Map_modes); docs/design/systems/economy.md cross-bloc scoreboard section (relative SoL is already designed as the contested quantity, so its map mode is pre-justified); UGS_MAPMODE=power already shipped per resources-and-grids.md.

findings.title: The information asymmetry between blocs is a UI feature, not just a sim feature — same dossier form, different columns
findings.detail: The locked architecture's most distinctive idea — the planner's dashboard shows plan data, not truth (falsified fulfillment reports) — is currently invisible because there is no dashboard to falsify. The region dossier is where it becomes playable: the planner's PRODUCTION block shows two columns, PLAN and REPORTED, with an AUDIT verb that (at legitimacy/attention cost) reveals a truer figure and can expose falsification; the market player's dossier shows one column of honest but LAGGED survey statistics stamped 'AS OF: Q1 1951' (statistics bureaus take a quarter). This is the single cheapest way to pass the pillar's own first-hour test at the UI layer: both blocs get the same teletype page, but the East reads reports it cannot fully trust and the West reads truth it receives late. It also inherits the war-legibility estimate rules wholesale: uncertain figures rounded to 2 significant figures, resampled per period so they never jitter, exact figures only for what you directly control. Foreign regions get the same dossier form filtered through espionage penetration — the inspector doubles as an intelligence product, which is period-perfect (CIA's actual Soviet-economy estimates were exactly this document).
findings.evidence: docs/research/economy-mechanics.md principles 7 and 10 ('the planner's dashboard shows plan data, not truth'); docs/research/war-legibility.md principle 5 (2-sig-fig ranges, period resampling, own-losses-exact — the rules transfer verbatim); docs/design/systems/economy.md planned-interface failure modes (audits/purges as internal espionage game); espionage pillar already shipped (commit e47a62e) providing the penetration numbers foreign-region dossiers would consume.

findings.title: Drill-down is a four-rung ladder with a sortable ledger as the workhorse, and regions become 'places' through ownership and memory
findings.detail: The working pattern across CK3 (county → holdings), Anno (island view), and this game's own war room is a strict ladder: HUD headline → national triage screen → place dossier → detail card, every rung linking both ways, no rung skippable-only-by-tooltip. The missing middle rung here is a NATIONAL ECONOMY LEDGER: one row per region (population, industry share, power factor, food ratio, constraint tag, monthly trend), sortable by any column, click-through to the dossier. Sorting IS the decision aid — 'sort by constraint severity, open the worst, allocate' is the entire monthly loop. Below it, the province card (already showing region name + power factor) stays the bottom rung. What makes a region a place rather than a row is what CK3 counties and Anno islands teach: persistent named things the player owns and remembers — deposits with size pips (Donbass COAL ●●●●●●●), named industrial complexes (Ruhr, Urals, Manchuria — already in the locked design), Great Projects under construction with timelines, and a short wire-history of the region's last few events. The wire itself is the top rung's glue: monthly economic events as teletype lines naming regions ('KUZBASS GRID DEFICIT — INDUSTRY THROTTLED 22%'), reusing THE WIRE component the war room already ships.
findings.evidence: docs/research/war-legibility.md 'what we implemented' (war room + THE WIRE + ticker as narrative memory — the component and the voice exist); docs/design/systems/economy.md industry section (named complexes are already the designated 'legible units'); CK3 county-holdings and Anno island-view pattern (persistent per-place screens with owned objects); [Game UI Database Frostpunk entries](https://www.gameuidatabase.com/gameData.php?id=38) for radial-hub drill-down reference.

findings.title: Negative space: monthly date-stamped figures, no per-tick display churn, and nothing without a verb or a why
findings.detail: Three deliberate omissions define the design as much as the content. (1) NO real-time numbers: the economy resolves monthly, so every dossier figure carries 'AS OF: 1 MAR 1951' and holds still between month boundaries — this prevents hypnotic number-watching (the 'watching a simulation' complaint is partly caused by wiggling numbers that invite watching), is free performance, and turns the dossier into a period document rather than a live feed. (2) NO per-province economics beyond the existing card: the research's hardest-won anti-pattern ('keep every dependency, delete every entity') applies to display too — showing per-province industry invites per-province wishes the game will rightly never grant, and 4,594-row anything is unreadable. (3) NO row without a verb or a why: every dossier line must either end in a trend arrow that links to an explanation or sit adjacent to a decision button; a stat that can do neither (raw permille internals, intermediate multipliers, the fixed-point plumbing) is cut. The one exception to 'always explain' is the planner's falsified data — where degraded information is the point, the UI must NOT offer a truth tooltip; the audit verb is the only path to truth, at a cost.
findings.evidence: docs/research/economy-mechanics.md principle 10 (attention as the scaled resource; 'every emergent outcome needs a why inspector, EXCEPT where degraded information is the point') and anti-patterns list (per-province queues); docs/research/war-legibility.md rule 'sample the fuzz once per period so numbers don't jitter' — the same stillness rule generalized to all economic display.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Region Dossier panel (the economic 'battle inspector')
mechanics_recommendations.why: Directly answers 'more information in regions'; makes the existing region data (cohorts, power, deposits, agriculture) inspectable in the game's teletype voice; is the surface where bloc asymmetry (plan-vs-reported columns, audit verb) becomes visible; reuses a UI pattern the codebase already shipped and validated for war.
mechanics_recommendations.how: State: a RegionSnapshot struct per region, recomputed on SimClock::new_month in TickSet::Economy after balances — { population_by_cohort, pop_trend_permille, power_gen, power_demand, power_factor, industry_output, industry_reported (planner: output * falsification_factor), grain_prod, grain_demand, deposits: Vec<(Commodity, size)>, constraint: ConstraintKind, constraint_severity_permille, wire_history: last 4 event lines }. Constraint = argmin over normalized limiters {power_factor, labor_ratio (urban workers vs workplaces), input_ratio (coal/steel availability), plan_allocation_share}; severity = 1000 - min. Assessment sentence templated from ConstraintKind + severity, ~50 lines exactly like the battle diagnosis. Panel opens from clicking a region name anywhere (province card, ledger, wire line, map). Layout: header (NAME / COUNTRY / POP 4.2M ▲ / 'COAL / HEAVY INDUSTRY'), four fixed blocks (PEOPLE, POWER with a gen-vs-demand bar, PRODUCTION with deposit pips and named complexes, FOOD with quota line), footer = BINDING CONSTRAINT + assessment + 2-3 contextual verb buttons (planner: ALLOCATE CONSTRUCTION / ADJUST QUOTA / AUDIT; market: no direct region verbs — buttons deep-link to the national parameter that most affects this region, keeping the asymmetry honest). All figures date-stamped 'AS OF <month>'. Foreign regions: same layout, values widened to 2-sig-fig ranges by espionage penetration, unknown blocks printed as 'NO COVERAGE'.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Binding-constraint model + BOTTLENECK map mode
mechanics_recommendations.why: The one-word answer to 'where does this month's construction decision go'; turns 250 regions into a glanceable triage map; showcases the locked architecture's migrating-constraint thesis (early game: power everywhere; late Soviet game: labor everywhere — the stagnation story told by a map mode).
mechanics_recommendations.how: The ConstraintKind computation from the snapshot (integer permille math, BTreeMap iteration, digest-tested). Map mode added to the M-cycle: province fill = categorical color by its region's ConstraintKind (power=amber, labor=blue, inputs=grey, food=green-red, none=dim), intensity stepped by severity band (3 bands, not continuous — chunky reads better and avoids implying false precision). Legend panel doubles as national summary with counts per constraint ('POWER-LIMITED: 14 REGIONS') and each legend row is a click-to-filter into the ledger. Constraint changes emit a wire line ('URALS NOW LABOR-LIMITED — RURAL RESERVE EXHAUSTED').

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: National Economy Ledger (sortable region triage table)
mechanics_recommendations.why: The missing middle rung between the country-scalar HUD and the region dossier; sorting is the actual decision aid for the once-a-month allocation; the natural home of the planner's PLAN/REPORTED discrepancy columns and the market player's tax-base view — one screen, two bloc-specific column sets.
mechanics_recommendations.how: A panel (extend UGS_PANEL=econ) listing the player's regions: NAME | POP | INDUSTRY | PWR% | FOOD% | CONSTRAINT | Δ (monthly trend glyph). Planner adds PLAN | REPORTED | audit-flag column; market adds TAX BASE | GROWTH (lagged one quarter). Click column header to sort (stable sort on the snapshot's fixed-point values — pure UI state, no sim impact); click row to open the dossier; click map-mode icon to jump to bottleneck mode centered on that region. Cap visible rows ~20 with the sort making the cap irrelevant (USSR ~15 regions fits whole; colonial empires scroll). Same table renders foreign countries through the espionage filter — this IS the intelligence estimate product.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Monthly Economic Briefing + economy wire integration
mechanics_recommendations.why: Gives the monthly cadence a ceremonial heartbeat (matching the locked 'one construction decision per game-month' and the ceremonial-pause plan moments); converts passive simulation output into a prompt for the month's decision; wire-service voice is the game's established identity.
mechanics_recommendations.how: On SimClock::new_month, generate 3-6 wire lines from snapshot deltas crossing thresholds (grid deficit onset, constraint change, food ratio under 950 permille, plan quarter fulfillment) into the existing wire component, each line carrying a RegionId for click-through. Optionally (setting, default on at speeds 1-2) an auto-pause BRIEFING card at month rollover: top 3 changes, worst 3 regions by constraint severity, plan/quarter status line, and one templated recommendation ('RECOMMEND: CONSTRUCTION TO KUZBASS (POWER)') — one ACKNOWLEDGE button and one button that jumps straight to the construction allocation. The recommendation must be derived from the same visible constraint data (never hidden logic) so the player can learn to beat it.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Verb-anchored readout rule (design constraint, enforced in review)
mechanics_recommendations.why: The complaint is 'autonomy AND information' — information alone deepens the watching-a-simulation feeling. A hard editorial rule keeps the inspector from bloating into Vic3.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Written into the design doc as an acceptance test per dossier row: every row must terminate in (a) a verb button, (b) a deep-link to the screen holding the relevant verb, or (c) a trend glyph whose click prints a one-line inline 'why' (no nested tooltips, ever — flat text expansion under the row). Rows failing all three are cut before implementation. Corollary: ship the dossier in the same slice as at least one region-targeted verb (region-targeted construction allocation is the obvious first, since construction-as-capacity-pool is already the locked design) — never ship the inspector alone.

pitfalls: Vic3's nested-tooltip archaeology: burying causes under hover-of-hover chains and window stacks. Everything explanatory prints inline as flat text in the dossier; a fact that needs three hovers to reach effectively does not exist. (This is also a real-time-with-pause issue: tooltips demand a still cursor; a paused player scanning 15 regions needs scannable pages.)

Map-mode and panel proliferation: adding a mode per commodity or a tab per subsystem because the data exists. Every mode/screen must name the decision made while looking at it; commodity detail lives in the dossier and ledger, not as eight coal-shaped map modes nobody opens twice.

Live-number hypnosis: displaying per-tick recomputed economics makes the player watch numbers wiggle — the literal 'watching a simulation' complaint rendered in UI. All economic display is monthly, date-stamped, and still between boundaries; uncertainty fuzz is sampled once per period (war-legibility rule 5) so estimates never jitter.

Symmetric chrome betraying the asymmetry pillar: if both blocs get the same dossier with the same buttons, the game's own first-hour test fails at the UI layer even with an asymmetric sim underneath. The plan/reported columns, the audit verb, the lagged-survey stamps, and the different verb sets are load-bearing — do not 'simplify' them away in v1.

Shipping the inspector without a verb: pure legibility work makes the sim MORE visibly autonomous and the player MORE visibly a spectator. The slice must pair the dossier/ledger with region-targeted construction allocation at minimum, so the first thing a player does with the new information is act on it.

False precision in foreign/reported data: printing '4,127,882 tons' for an espionage estimate or a falsified report destroys the fiction and misleads the player. Two significant figures for anything not directly controlled; exact figures only for the player's own true, current holdings.
analysts.first_hour_test: A new player boots the USSR, presses the econ key. They do not see a country scalar — they see the LEDGER: fifteen named regions (MOSCOW, DONBASS, URALS, KUZBASS, BAKU...), each with population, industry, PWR%, FOOD%, a one-word constraint tag, and a trend glyph; two rows carry an amber POWER-LIMITED tag. One keystroke flips the map to BOTTLENECK mode and the same two regions glow amber on the map — the numbers have places. They click URALS and get a one-page teletype dossier: 'AS OF 1 JAN 1950 — POP 3.4M ▲ — COAL / HEAVY INDUSTRY', a generation-vs-demand bar visibly short, deposit pips, and the footer sentence 'OUTPUT LIMITED BY POWER: GENERATION COVERS 82% OF DEMAND', followed by an ALLOCATE CONSTRUCTION button. That button is the first economic decision: point this month's construction capacity at Urals generation. They unpause; at the February rollover the briefing card reports 'URALS GENERATION +6% — CONSTRAINT UNCHANGED' and the wire prints 'KUZBASS GRID DEFICIT — INDUSTRY THROTTLED 22%', prompting month two's decision. It feels like playing rather than watching because the loop is closed and legible: a named place reported a named problem, the player answered it with a verb, and the next month's document graded the answer. The same player noticing the PLAN/REPORTED column pair — and the AUDIT button beside it — learns in minute ten that their own dashboard can lie to them. Booting the USA instead: the identical dossier form, but figures stamped 'SURVEY, Q4 1949', no allocate button on the region — the verbs are interest rates, procurement contracts, and tax parameters at the national screen, with the dossier deep-linking to them. Same page, different columns, different verbs: the pillar's asymmetry is visible in the first hour without reading a single tooltip."

findings.title: The regional substrate already exists but is frozen at init — thawing it is the whole move
findings.detail: In /Users/erikrahtjen/Code/personal/untitled-grand-strategy/crates/ugs-sim/src/economy.rs, `EconomyStatic.region_industry` distributes country industry to regions by urban-population share exactly once (lines 148–180) and never changes again; meanwhile `Economies.industry` in planning.rs grows the country scalar monthly. So regional industry shares are permanently 1950-shaped no matter what the player does, and nothing the player does can ever be ABOUT a place. The minimal v1 slice is therefore not 'regionalize the economy' but 'make region_industry mutable and let exactly one new verb mutate it': promote it to a serialized `RegionalIndustry` resource (centi-points per region, folded into the digest), make country industry the derived sum for dashboards/misreporting, and keep everything else (quotas, market levers, balances) national. Power capacity/demand formulas already read region_industry, so a region that grows immediately draws more power and shifts its factor — the feedback loop is already wired, it just has constant inputs today.
findings.evidence: crates/ugs-sim/src/economy.rs:120-180 (static distribution, `initialized` latch); crates/ugs-sim/src/planning.rs:230-241 (production already computes country power factor FROM regional factors, weighted by region_industry — the plumbing for regional consequences exists)

findings.title: The military-command layer is the proven template for watching-to-playing; copy its shape, not new machinery
findings.detail: The same complaint ('sim runs fine, nothing to DO') was fixed for the war pillar with a specific pattern: the player decides what exists, where it is based, and the directive; the sim executes placement ('The player never moves a division directly'). Formations cost the existing military_stock — 'no new economy state' was an explicit design constraint there. The economic equivalent: the player decides which PROJECTS exist and in which region; the sim executes the growth. Investment output (invest_out, planning.rs:287) currently converts to industry uniformly and invisibly; redirect it through a per-country construction pool that drains into 2–3 concurrent named projects, with any surplus auto-investing exactly as today. That last clause is the AI-default guardrail for free: all 226 countries and any player who ignores the system get today's behavior unchanged, and projects are pure upside agency, not a chore.
findings.evidence: docs/design/systems/military-command.md ('State' section: 'IndustryState.military_stock (already accumulating) is now spent — no new economy state'); crates/ugs-sim/src/planning.rs:287-294 (invest_out → INVEST_CONVERT_PERMILLE is the hook point)

findings.title: A region inspector is ~85% presentation-only; the sim already holds nearly everything a dossier card needs
findings.detail: The app already has province click-selection (`Selected` in crates/ugs-app/src/map.rs:32) and a province info card reading Demographics. A region dossier needs: name (RegionDef.name), owner (EconomyStatic.region_owner), industry points (region_industry), full power status — capacity/generation/demand/factor (RegionalPower.by_region), population cohorts (sum province Demographics over the region), deposits (re-aggregate ProvinceDef.deposits by region instead of by country — a one-time app-side or init-time BTreeMap), nuclear facilities (NuclearPrograms.site_region already matches regions and already loads grids), and active project (the one new piece). Only two genuinely new sim items are required for legibility: per-region deposit sums (trivial, computed at init next to region_owner) and the project list. Everything else is UI over existing deterministic state — meaning the inspector can ship in the same PR as the map mode with near-zero sim risk.
findings.evidence: crates/ugs-app/src/map.rs:32,593-609 (Selected + selection-driven info refresh); crates/ugs-sim/src/economy.rs:93-118 (PowerStatus per region, already a map mode); crates/ugs-sim/src/economy.rs:239-252 (nuclear plants already keyed to region)
