findings.title: Construction gated by inputs it cannot buy is both the locked architecture and the genre's loudest lesson
findings.detail: Locked principle 2 ('never one self-purchasing currency') exists because HoI4's civ-factory snowball and Victoria 3's construction-sector buildings both collapsed into a solved build-more-builders loop — Victoria 3 players describe the queue as 'everything constrained by construction points that don't react to the economy' and petitioned to end it. The v1 pool must therefore accrue from invest_out but be THROTTLED by the existing material ratios (coal_ratio, later steel/cement) and by the regional power factor of the project's host region — so a project in a blacked-out region builds slowly, which is itself legible in the inspector ('progress slowed: power 62%'). This costs zero new commodities: both throttles are computed monthly today. It also produces the campaign-arc the doc wants: early game the pool is materials-bound, late game labor/power-bound, and the binding constraint migrating is the story.
findings.evidence: docs/research/economy-mechanics.md principles 1-2; Paradox forum 'Petition to end the construction queue mechanic' (https://forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/petition-to-end-the-construction-queue-mechanic.1594102/); Victoria 3 wiki Building page (https://vic3.paradoxwikis.com/Building); crates/ugs-sim/src/planning.rs:264-268 (materials ratio already clamped 500-1000 and applied to output)

findings.title: The asymmetry thesis survives regionalization only if the two blocs get DIFFERENT regional verbs
findings.detail: The command layer already rejects wrong-interface commands (set_planned_allocation refuses market countries, planning.rs:347-368, with a test), so the enforcement pattern exists. Planned economies should place any project directly — quantities: 'a steel combine in the Urals, now' — with the ceremonial framing (project start is a wire notice, a named thing). Market economies must NOT place industry: they place public goods only (power authorities, infrastructure) and designate incentive zones (a tax-relief permille on a region), while private growth auto-allocates each month to the regions with the best conditions (power surplus, urban labor, incentives) via a published, deterministic scoring formula — parameters, with the inspector showing 'private investment attracted this month and why'. This makes the first-hour contrast concrete at the REGIONAL level, where today it only exists in the levers panel. It also preserves the epistemic asymmetry: the planned inspector must show reported/plan figures consistent with the national padding logic, not leak truth the planner's own dashboard hides.
findings.evidence: crates/ugs-sim/src/planning.rs:347-388 + test wrong_interface_commands_are_rejected; docs/design/systems/economy.md ('planner sets quantities... market sets parameters'; misreporting: 'the dashboard shows plan data, not truth')

findings.title: Every v1 project type must land on an existing consumer, or the slice ships parallel instead of connected
findings.detail: The audit of existing consumers: military_stock accrues from output × military share (spent by RaiseFormation and upkeep); power factor_permille throttles output and is a map mode; agriculture yield_permille multiplies grain; grain ratio drives famine-adjacent SoL; nuclear programs load their host region's grid. Four project types cover all of them with no new sinks: INDUSTRIAL EXPANSION (+RegionalIndustry → more national output → more military_stock at the same permille, and more regional power demand — a real tradeoff), POWER STATION (+built_power added into the region's capacity formula → factor relief → output and nuclear-program relief), AGRICULTURAL MECHANIZATION (+country or region yield_permille → grain ratio → the existing food section of the panel), and GREAT PROJECTS (scripted named entries — Volga-Don, Aswan bid, Interstate — same machinery, bigger cost, influence/legitimacy payout on completion, per the locked doc). Nothing new to consume the outputs is needed; the war systems, grids, and agriculture already do.
findings.evidence: crates/ugs-sim/src/planning.rs:285-288 (military_stock accrual), crates/ugs-sim/src/economy.rs:232-260 (capacity/demand formulas ready for a built_power and dynamic industry term), crates/ugs-sim/src/agriculture.rs (yield_permille hook); docs/design/systems/economy.md Construction bullet (named Great Projects with influence payouts)

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: RegionalIndustry: promote region industry from init-time constant to first-class dynamic sim state
mechanics_recommendations.why: It is the single change that makes regions places where things can HAPPEN. Without it the inspector shows a museum; with it every other mechanic (projects, power, private investment flow) has something to move. It is also what the locked architecture ('industry chain at regional resolution') requires eventually — doing it now with the current one-good abstraction means no rework later, only refinement.
mechanics_recommendations.how: New serialized resource `RegionalIndustry { by_region: BTreeMap<RegionId, u64 /* centi-points */> }`, seeded from the existing urban-share distribution at init, folded into the determinism digest and savegame. `update_production` computes each country's output as the sum over its regions of `region_centi * region_power_factor/1000 * materials/1000 * held/1000` (replacing the country-average power factor — sharper and already computable from RegionalPower), keeps growth/depreciation national in aggregate but applies depreciation per-region proportionally. `Economies.IndustryState.actual_centi` becomes the derived sum (kept as a cache for dashboards, misreporting, and intel, refreshed monthly). Occupation already filters by province holder; regional resolution makes 'the Donbas is overrun' a visible regional loss instead of a national haircut.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Construction pool + project slots: the one new player verb, through the command queue at monthly cadence
mechanics_recommendations.why: This converts the invisible invest_out trickle into decisions with names and places — the exact fix the military layer proved — while the surplus-auto-invest default keeps all AI countries and passive players on today's behavior with zero new AI code in v1. Slot caps are the decision budget: 2 generic slots + 1 Great Project slot means roughly one meaningful choice per month at Great Power scale, per the locked cadence.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Resource `Construction { pool_centi: BTreeMap<CountryTag, u64>, projects: BTreeMap<ProjectId, Project>, next_id: u32 }` with `Project { owner: CountryTag, region: RegionId, kind: ProjectKind, cost_centi: u64, progress_centi: u64, started_tick: u64 }`; `ProjectKind { IndustrialExpansion, PowerStation, AgriMechanization, Great(GreatProjectId) }`. Monthly, after update_production: `pool += invest_out * DIRECTED_SHARE_PERMILLE / 1000` (start at ~500‰; the other half auto-converts as today so baseline growth persists); pool drains equally into active projects, each project's intake further scaled by its host region's `factor_permille` and the country materials ratio (the cannot-buy-itself gate). Completion: IndustrialExpansion adds `SIZE_CENTI` to RegionalIndustry[region]; PowerStation adds to a new `built_power: BTreeMap<RegionId, u64>` read by the capacity formula (`capacity = industry * POWER_CAP_PER_INDUSTRY + POWER_CAP_BASE + built_power`); AgriMechanization bumps the owner's yield_permille via the existing Agriculture resource; Great projects additionally fire a wire notice and an influence/legitimacy payout. Commands: `StartProject { country, region, kind }` (validated: region owned AND currently held, slot free, kind legal for the country's EconomicSystem), `CancelProject { country, id }` (refund nothing or 50% — pick one, tune later). All BTreeMap iteration, all integer math, costs in a `construction::tuning` module.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Asymmetric regional verbs: planned places quantities, market places parameters + public goods
mechanics_recommendations.why: The pillar's acid test is that the blocs feel different in the first hour, and today the difference lives only in three abstract levers. Regionalized verbs make it physical: the Soviet player points at the Urals and decrees a combine; the American player cannot — they build the power and cut the taxes and watch Texas grow. Supreme Ruler's failure ('communism = capitalism with modifiers') is the anti-pattern this dodges.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Planned countries: `StartProject` accepts all ProjectKinds; project starts print ceremonial wire notices; regional inspector shows REPORTED regional figures (pad the regional view with the same national padding factor applied proportionally, so the planner's map lies consistently with their dashboard). Market countries: `StartProject` accepts only PowerStation/Great (public works); new command `SetDevelopmentZone { country, region, on: bool }` (cap ~3 zones) applies an incentive weight; monthly, a deterministic private-investment pass distributes `invest_out * PRIVATE_SHARE / 1000` across the country's regions scored by `w = urban_k * factor_permille * (1000 + ZONE_BONUS_PERMILLE * zone) / 1000` (published formula, integer, sorted BTreeMap iteration), adding directly to RegionalIndustry. Inspector for market regions shows 'private investment this month: N (power 98%, zone active)' so parameter play is legible. Reuse the wrong-interface rejection pattern from set_planned_allocation verbatim.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Region dossier + economy map mode: legibility layer over existing state
mechanics_recommendations.why: Half the complaint is 'more information in regions'; most of the answer already exists in RegionalPower, Demographics, deposits, and nuclear site data and just has no surface. The dossier is also where the play loop closes: the map mode must answer 'where is the problem', the dossier 'why', and the project menu 'what can I do about it' — the Vic2-opacity lesson from the research doc (every emergent outcome needs a why-inspector).
mechanics_recommendations.how: App-side: extend the existing `Selected` province flow to resolve `province.region` and render a region card: name, owner, industry (from RegionalIndustry; reported-padded for planned self-view), power bar (capacity/generation/demand/factor from PowerStatus), population (sum cohorts over region provinces, cached per month), deposits (new init-time `region_deposits: BTreeMap<RegionId, BTreeMap<DepositKind,u64>>` beside region_owner in EconomyStatic — sim-side but 5 lines), nuclear facility line if any program's site_region matches, active project with progress bar and 'slowed by' cause. New `UGS_MAPMODE=econ`: regions shaded by industry density, red hatching where factor_permille < 900, project markers (hammer icon) on regions with active builds. Bottleneck classification (power-bound / materials-bound / occupied) computed in the app from existing ratios — presentation-only, no sim state.

pitfalls: Build-queue creep: if project slots scale with industry, the US player is running 15 concurrent builds by 1960 and this is HoI4's construction tab with extra steps. Hard-cap slots (2 generic + 1 Great, maybe +1 via a late policy) and make projects CHUNKY (multi-month, named, wire-noticed) — the decision budget is the design, not a tuning afterthought. Refuse per-region quota requests in the same spirit: quotas stay national permille forever; regions are acted on only through projects and zones.

Determinism/save regressions: RegionalIndustry and Construction must be serialized, folded into a digest, and iterated as BTreeMaps; project completion order within a month must be by ProjectId, not insertion accident. Old saves lacking the new resources must load with the init-time distribution (the same latch pattern EconomyStatic uses). Run the determinism-check skill after; the mid-war fixture save (saves/war-jul-1950.ron) must still load.

Leaking truth through the new surfaces: the planned player's regional inspector must show padded figures consistent with reported_centi, and foreign players' view of rival regions must go through the existing observed_industry_centi penetration logic — otherwise the region map mode becomes a free intel bypass and quietly deletes both the misreporting mechanic and a chunk of the espionage pillar.

Power stations trivializing the throttle: if a cheap PowerStation erases any deficit in two months, the grid system stops being a strategic geography and becomes a whack-a-mole errand. Cost power capacity so full electrification of a starved region is a multi-year commitment competing with industry itself, and keep the coal-coupling (generation still scales with coal ratio) so building plants without fuel visibly underdelivers.

The market side degenerating into 'planned with fewer buttons': if private allocation is invisible or random-feeling, market players will experience LESS agency than before. The scoring formula must be published in-UI ('simple, published, and correct' per the design doc), the inspector must attribute every month's private growth to its causes, and zones must visibly redirect it within 2-3 months — parameter play only works when the response is legible and prompt.
analysts.first_hour_test: Boot as the USSR, January 1950. Press the economy map mode: regions shade by industrial weight — Moscow, the Donbas, the Urals glow; red hatching marks grids running throttled. Click the Urals: a dossier card names the region, shows 14.2 industry points, POWER 71% (generation 180 / demand 253), 4.1M urban / 9.8M rural, coal and iron deposits, and NO ACTIVE PROJECT. The econ panel now has a CONSTRUCTION section: pool accruing ~9 pts/month from the 45% investment quota, 0/2 slots used. The first decision writes itself from what the map showed: the Urals' industry is losing 29% of its output to the grid — start a POWER STATION there (6 months), or gamble bigger and drop an INDUSTRIAL EXPANSION into fully-powered Kuzbass instead; the wire prints 'COUNCIL OF MINISTERS DECREES URALS POWER PROGRAM'. Next month the pool drains, the progress bar moves, and when it completes the red hatching fades and national output ticks up BECAUSE OF a place the player chose. It feels like playing rather than watching because the loop is see-a-place, diagnose-its-bottleneck, commit-capital, watch-the-map-change — the sim still solves everything, but where it improves is authored. Boot as the USA and the same inspector shows Pittsburgh at 99% power with 'PRIVATE INVESTMENT THIS MONTH: +0.4 (power surplus, urban labor)'; the project menu offers only public works, and the first decision is a development zone on the throttled Tennessee Valley region plus an interest-rate cut — then watching private capital actually move there, which is a different game, which is the pillar.

analysts.analyst: projects-as-agency (discrete named projects as the unit of economic decision-making)

findings.title: Decisions feel like governing because they are state-gated and resource-priced; focuses feel like a menu because they are script-ordered and time-priced
findings.detail: The HoI4 'Decisive Action' dev diary is explicit that decisions were added because focus trees are 'rigidly tied to the design of the tree and never very dynamic' — every focus costs the same abstract currency (70 days), arrives in an author-fixed order, and is available regardless of what the sim is doing. Decisions instead appear when conditions in the world are true and cost fungible things (PP, equipment, states). That is the whole difference: a focus answers 'what does the script offer next', a decision answers 'what does MY situation demand'. For UGS this means the project system must never be a tech-tree-shaped catalog you walk down every campaign. A project offer should exist because a specific region's state makes it real: the Lower Volga has a river gradient and a power-deficit grid, so a dam is offerable there; Kazakhstan has idle arable land and the country has a grain shortfall, so Virgin Lands surfaces. Historical projects are pinned to their real regions with real open dates, but the OFFER is a predicate over sim state, so campaigns diverge and choosing feels like responding to your country rather than consuming content.
findings.evidence: HoI4 dev diary 'Decisive Action' (https://forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/developer-diary/hoi4-dev-diary-decisive-action.1053930/) — decisions exist to escape the 70-day script; community critique thread 'National Focus trees are overrated' (https://forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/why-do-i-think-national-focus-trees-are-overrated.1467006/) independently converges on the same diagnosis.

findings.title: Projects are the missing NOUN that makes regions legible — anchor region inspection to named construction, the way Stellaris anchors it to megastructures and Civ to wonders
findings.detail: The player complaint is 'nothing to DO, nowhere to LOOK'. Regions today are data with one map mode. A named project gives a region a face: a site pin on the map, a progress ring, a monthly line in the wire, and a reason to open the region panel at all (the panel answers 'why is MY dam slow' — because this grid is throttled, this cement flow is short, this labor pool is drained by the army). Stellaris megastructures work not because of their bonuses but because they are visible on the galaxy map for decades while building — other players SEE your commitment. Civ wonders add the race: someone else can finish first and your investment is partially lost. Both properties transfer: a Great Project should render on the strategic map for every country that has intel on it (tying into the espionage pillar's four domains — a rival's enrichment plant progress is exactly the kind of thing intel networks report), and contested projects (Aswan, the Indian steel plants) are literally races. The region panel v1 should be: demography strip, grid status, commodity balances, industry complexes, and — at the top — active/offerable projects, because projects are the only rows with a verb attached.
findings.evidence: Stellaris megastructure design (multi-stage, decade-scale, map-visible commitments — https://stellaris.paradoxwikis.com/Megastructures); Civilization wonder-race loss aversion is 30 years of proven drama; UGS docs/design/systems/economy.md already names complexes (Ruhr, Urals) as 'the legible units' — projects extend that principle from stocks to changes-in-progress.

findings.title: Commitment must be flow-denominated (monthly draws from regional pools), not lump-sum — that is what welds projects to the substrate and makes overruns emergent instead of RNG
findings.detail: A project priced as a one-time cost is a shop purchase; a project priced as '18% of national construction capacity + 40kt cement/mo + 15kt steel/mo from the Volga region for 30 months' is a standing claim against the same pools everything else wants, which is exactly how the locked architecture defines construction (capacity consumed as a flow, gated by inputs it cannot buy itself). Then most overruns need no dice: the cement flow fell short for four months, so the bar moved slower, and the wire can say WHY. Vic3 journal entries demonstrate that a progress bar with visible advancing/blocking conditions reads as a situation, not a timer; Terra Invicta demonstrates the other half — its engineering projects compete with everything else for the same boost/money income, so starting one is felt everywhere. Reserve stochastic overruns (SimRng fork per project id) for the flavorful minority — geology surprises, purged engineers, sabotage — and always attribute them in the wire. An unattributed overrun is noise; an attributed one is a story and, for sabotage, a counterintelligence prompt.
findings.evidence: Vic3 journal entries as condition-driven progress (https://vic3.paradoxwikis.com/Journal); Terra Invicta Council Engineering Projects drawing on shared faction income (https://terrainvictagame.fandom.com/wiki/Council_Engineering_Projects); UGS economy.md lines 47-51 already specify construction as a flow gated by cement+steel+labor.

findings.title: The cross-pillar payload is historically native, not bolted on — Aswan IS influence warfare, gulag canals ARE the planned asymmetry, enrichment IS escalation
findings.detail: The Aswan record is a complete game loop that actually happened: the West offered ~$70M in Dec 1955 explicitly because of the Czech arms deal (an influence-warfare counter-move), Dulles withdrew in July 1956 over Nasser's alignment, the USSR stepped in, and the backlash contributed to Suez. That is: contested bid → conditional funding → withdrawal penalty → rival completion payout → crisis. Model it as an auction with a withdrawal-backlash mechanic and you have the influence pillar's best economic verb for free. Likewise the Soviet 'Great Construction Projects of Communism' (Volga-Don, Turkmen Canal, Kuibyshev/Stalingrad dams) were built with GULAG labor — ~1.5M prisoners through the three canals — which is the planned interface's crash-surge signature move (output now, welfare/legitimacy debt later) already listed in economy.md. And enrichment plants (Paducah 1951, Novouralsk expansion) are grid-scale power consumers per the locked architecture, so a 'build the second diffusion plant' project is simultaneously an economy decision, an escalation milestone, and the espionage pillar's richest target. Every catalog entry should declare its payloads: influence stream, intel footprint, escalation weight, sabotage surface.
findings.evidence: Aswan financing sequence: history.com (https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/july-19/united-states-withdraws-offer-of-aid-for-aswan-dam), ADST oral histories (https://adst.org/2016/06/dont-give-dam-feud-financing-aswan-high-dam/), FRUS 1955-57 vol XIV; Great Construction Projects of Communism (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Construction_Projects_of_Communism) and gulag canal labor figures (Jamestown, https://jamestown.org/volga-don-canal-last-great-stalin-project-desperately-needs-updating-or-replacement/).

findings.title: One catalog, two verbs: the planned player COMMANDS projects, the market player AUTHORIZES and FUNDS them — or the asymmetry thesis dies at the project screen
findings.detail: The tempting design — both blocs pick a project card and assign capacity — would quietly convert the pillar's thesis into a skin. The historical instruments differ: the Interstate Highway System was the 1956 act creating the Highway Trust Fund (a financing parameter — fuel tax revenue, matching formula), not Eisenhower allocating cement; St. Lawrence Seaway needed years of Congressional appropriation fights. So: the planned player selects a project at a plan session and directly pledges quantities (capacity share, commodity quotas, optionally forced-labor surge), and its failure modes are shortage cascades and falsified progress reports (the dashboard shows the padded number, consistent with the misreporting mechanic already shipped). The market player instead AUTHORIZES a project (a legislative decision with a political cost tied to stability/legitimacy) and sets its funding parameters (appropriation level, bond issuance, cost-plus vs fixed-price contracting); private contractors then bid capacity in, speed responds to funding level and the business cycle, and the failure modes are cost inflation and funding fights, not material shortage. Same substrate, same progress bar, different verbs, different ways to fail — which is exactly the first-hour differentiation test the economy doc sets.
findings.evidence: UGS docs/design/systems/economy.md (quantities-vs-parameters thesis) and planning-interfaces.md (misreporting shows REPORTED to the planned player); Federal-Aid Highway Act 1956 / Highway Trust Fund structure; St. Lawrence Seaway authorization history (approved 1954 after decades of failed bills, opened 1959).

findings.title: Cadence math supports 2-4 concurrent domestic projects plus 0-2 foreign bids — the ledger, not the map, is where monthly attention lands
findings.detail: The architecture budgets ~one construction decision per game-month. At real project durations (Volga-Don ~4 years, Kuibyshev dam 7 years, Seaway 5 years), a portfolio of 2-4 concurrent projects generates roughly one meaningful event per month across the portfolio: a groundbreaking, a milestone (each project should have 2-4 named stages, Stellaris-style, each with its own completion line — 'first turbine spinning at Tsimlyansk' months before the canal opens), an overrun report demanding a response (accept delay / surge / cut another draw), or a completion ceremony. That is precisely real-time-with-pause pacing: the wire interrupts, the player pauses, opens the project ledger or the region, makes one chunky choice, resumes. More than ~4 concurrent projects and events blur back into watching a simulation; fewer than 2 and months go silent. Cap concurrency by an explicit named constraint (Gosplan attention / Congressional calendar) rather than a soft resource, so the player understands why they cannot greenlight everything — scarcity of slots is what makes choosing one project a statement about national priorities, which is the feeling the pillar is for.
findings.evidence: UGS economy.md line 49 ('~One construction decision per game-month'); Stellaris multi-stage megastructure pacing; the military-command layer precedent in this project (same complaint, solved with a bounded decision surface).

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Condition-gated project offers (the Offer Board), not an era menu
mechanics_recommendations.why: Kills focus-tree-ification. A project you can always build is a shop item; a project that surfaces because your regions' state makes it real is governing. Also the cheapest way to make regions inspectable: the offer names the region and the deficits it answers.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Each catalog entry in RON: site (region id or predicate over region state: river-class terrain, grid deficit > X, arable-unused > Y), open window (earliest date, optional historical date for AI bias), prerequisites (tech era, relations for foreign bids), costs (capacity share permille, per-commodity monthly draws, duration in months, labor draw from region cohorts), payloads (grid MW, industry method unlock, agriculture modifier, influence stream, escalation weight, intel footprint), and risk profile (overrun class, sabotage surface). Monthly, in TickSet::Economy, evaluate predicates over BTreeMap-ordered regions; newly-true offers emit a wire item and appear on the Offer Board (a tab of the econ panel and a pin on the map). Offers can expire or be claimed by AI countries — rejected history is possible.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: The Project Ledger: slot-capped portfolio with flow-denominated commitments and staged milestones
mechanics_recommendations.why: This is the economic-agency slice itself — the place the player looks weekly and acts monthly. Flow pricing welds projects to the shared pools so shortages elsewhere become attributable delays here; stages guarantee the wire has something true to say between groundbreaking and ribbon-cutting.
mechanics_recommendations.how: State per active project: stage index, progress (fixed-point work-units), committed draws {construction_permille, cement_t_mo, steel_t_mo, labor}, actuals last month, overrun ledger (list of {cause, months} — causes: input shortage, labor shortage, sabotage, geology, purge). Monthly: satisfied_fraction = min over inputs of (delivered/committed); progress += base_rate * satisfied_fraction; stochastic events from rng.fork(b"projects") forked again by project id, probability scaled by risk profile and (for planned) recent purge/surge flags. Concurrency cap 3 (tunable, named 'Gosplan portfolio' / 'the President's program'); starting a 4th requires suspending one (sunk progress decays slowly, not lost). Stages (2-4 per project) each carry partial payloads. On completion: ceremony modal at pause, permanent payload applied, influence pulse to observers scaled by information penetration. Planned-only response verbs: Crash Surge (progress x1.5 for 6 months, region SoL and unrest debt, gulag-labor flavor); Falsify (the reported bar advances, the true one doesn't — audit mechanic already sketched catches it). Market-only: Raise Appropriation (more budget/inflation pressure), Rebid Contract (reset cost inflation, lose 2 months).

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Contested Foreign Bids (the Aswan auction) as the influence pillar's economic verb
mechanics_recommendations.why: Historically this is where economic systems competition was actually fought in the third world, and it gives the market player projects with geopolitical teeth without betraying the parameter interface (a bid is a financing offer). It also creates the game's best scripted-feeling emergent drama: withdrawal backlash → host swings to rival → rival builds a monument in your former client.
mechanics_recommendations.how: A foreign project offer (Aswan High Dam, Bhilai/Rourkela/Durgapur steel plants in India, Kariba Dam, Palace of Culture as intra-bloc gift) opens to all great powers meeting a relations threshold with the host. Bidding = committing hard currency (market: loans/grants with condition flags; planned: barter — machine tools and engineers, costing your own capacity pool). Host AI picks by weighted alignment + generosity + conditions attached. Winner runs the project remotely (host provides labor, winner provides capacity slice + commodities + engineers — who are then espionage assets/targets in-country). While building: monthly influence stream in the host region. Withdraw mid-project: large influence backlash, host relations collapse, rival gets a discounted re-bid window (the Suez loop). Completion: large permanent influence payout + the payload accrues to the HOST's region — you are buying alignment, not GDP.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Map and wire presence: site pins, a Construction map mode, and attributed milestone events
mechanics_recommendations.why: 'Nowhere to LOOK' is half the complaint. Projects must be objects on the map you can click, not rows in a panel — and every delay must arrive with its cause attached, or the overrun system reads as dice.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Site pin at the project's region anchor province: icon by type (dam/canal/plant/rail/enrichment), progress ring, small flag of the builder (matters for foreign bids). Construction map mode tints regions by committed capacity share and flags starved projects red. Clicking a pin opens the region panel scrolled to the project card: stage bar, committed vs delivered draws (the legibility moment — 'cement 62% delivered, source: Donbas region, cause: rail link severed'), overrun ledger, response verbs. Wire items: offer surfaced, groundbreaking, each stage completion, any month with satisfied_fraction < 0.8 (batched, attributed), sabotage discovered (feeds counterintel), rival project intel (through the espionage penetration model — you see THEIR pins at the fidelity your networks earn), completion ceremony. Foreign-visible progress uses the intel system's existing fidelity tiers rather than ground truth.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Projects as espionage/escalation surfaces (declared payloads, not special cases)
mechanics_recommendations.why: The pillars stay welded only if project data declares its cross-pillar hooks so the other systems consume them generically — the enrichment plant should need zero bespoke code to be an intel target, a grid consumer, and an escalation step.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Payload fields consumed by existing systems: intel_footprint (raises the project's visibility in the rival's economic-intel domain; enrichment and launch complexes highest), sabotage_surface (covert-ops action 'Industrial Sabotage' targets an active project, on success appends an overrun-ledger entry with cause=sabotage(hidden until discovered)), escalation_weight (completion of enrichment/test-site/DEW-line projects shifts the tension/first-strike calculus already modeled), grid_delta and commodity_method payloads apply to the region's existing grid and industry state. The nuclear pipeline in economy.md then becomes literally a chain of Great Projects (diffusion plant → test site → weaponization complex → launch sites), giving the escalation pillar its economic spine for free.

pitfalls: Focus-tree-ification: if every campaign's project sequence is the same, the system collapses into a menu with extra steps. Guard: offers are predicates over sim state, several are mutually exclusive or claimable by AI rivals, and the historical date is an AI bias, not a player gate. Playtest check: do two campaigns as the same country produce different ledgers by 1955?

Unattributed overruns read as slot-machine noise. Every month of delay must carry a cause the player can click through to (input shortage names the source region and why; sabotage is hidden until counterintel finds it, then becomes a story). If the wire cannot explain a delay, the delay should not happen.

Symmetric verbs kill the pillar: giving the market player the planned player's 'assign capacity' command turns the asymmetry thesis into a UI skin. The market side must reach projects through authorization + funding parameters and contractor behavior, even though it is more work to build.

Portfolio spam or starvation: uncapped concurrency returns to watching a simulation (twelve bars creep); a cap of 1 makes months silent. Start at 3 domestic slots + 2 foreign bids and tune against the one-decision-per-month budget.

Determinism hazards specific to this system: per-project RNG must fork from SimRng with the project id as a stable label (never iteration order); offer evaluation must iterate regions in BTreeMap order; AI bid resolution must sort bidders by CountryTag before weighted selection; falsified progress must keep true and reported progress as separate deterministic tracks.

Payload inflation: if project rewards are percentage modifiers, projects become HoI4 focuses (invisible buffs). Every payload should be a step-change object the substrate already models — MW on a named grid, a production method, an influence stream, a rail link — never '+5% factory output'.
analysts.first_hour_test: Boot as the USSR, January 1st 1950, press E. The panel's new Projects tab shows a ledger with one active project the player did not start: the Volga-Don Canal, stage 2 of 3, 61% — because it was really under construction that month — drawing 120‰ of construction capacity and cement from the Lower Volga region, whose pin on the map carries a progress ring. The Offer Board below it shows two live offers surfaced by real region state: the Kuibyshev Hydroelectric Station (Middle Volga grid is power-deficit — the offer card says so) and the Main Turkmen Canal (Stalin's pet, huge draw, high overrun class — the trap is priced on the card). The first economic DECISION: the cement flow supports Volga-Don plus ONE of these. The player clicks the Kuibyshev pin, sees the Middle Volga region panel for the first time — grid at 87% throttle, cement balance, labor cohorts — and greenlights the dam at a plan session, pledging quantities. Two game-months later the wire reports cement delivery at 71% (Donbas shortfall, attributed), and the player chooses: accept the delay, or Crash Surge with gulag labor and eat the unrest debt. That is playing, not watching: the player made a portfolio choice under a visible constraint, learned to read a region to make it, and now owns the consequences by name. The US mirror: the St. Lawrence Seaway offer is live but grayed pending authorization — the player's verb is to push the authorization decision and set the appropriation level, then watch contractors bid capacity in; the same first hour teaches that the other bloc reaches the same catalog through different hands. Ship catalog (~20): USSR domestic — Volga-Don Canal (active at start), Kuibyshev HPP, Stalingrad HPP, Main Turkmen Canal (the prestige trap; cancellable on succession), Great Transformation of Nature shelterbelts, Virgin Lands Campaign (gated on grain shortfall, 1954+), Moscow Metro/vysotki prestige stage, Obninsk NPP (first nuclear power, influence pulse), Novouralsk enrichment expansion, Baikonur launch complex (1955+). US domestic — St. Lawrence Seaway (joint with Canada), Interstate Highway System (funding-parameter flagship, 1956), Paducah gaseous diffusion plant, Glen Canyon/Upper Colorado, Shippingport NPP, DEW Line (escalation payload), TAT-1 transatlantic cable (intel/influence payload). Contested foreign bids — Aswan High Dam (the set piece), Bhilai vs Rourkela vs Durgapur steel plants in India (three-way bid), Kariba Dam, Palace of Culture Warsaw (intra-bloc gift), Atoms-for-Peace reactor exports (repeatable small bid, seeds proliferation).

analysts.analyst: construction-agency (genre study: HoI4, EU4, Stellaris, Terra Invicta, Victoria 3, Workers & Resources: Soviet Republic)

findings.title: W&R's magic is traceable causality, not entity count — steal the diagnosability, not the vehicles
findings.detail: What planned-economy fans praise in Workers & Resources is not the trucks — it's that every idle factory has a discoverable reason (no workers, no power, no inputs, no transport link), and fixing the bottleneck makes the chain visibly 'hum'. Reviews consistently land on 'once your city starts to connect and hum, that's when immense satisfaction sets in.' The economy-mechanics research already says 'keep every dependency, delete every entity' — but the deleted entities must leave their legibility behind. At 250-region altitude that means every region carries a computed stock-flow ledger AND a one-line bottleneck verdict ('Ural steel at 78%: electricity throttled'). The player's complaint ('watching a simulation') is exactly what W&R avoids: its sim is fully inspectable, and every inspection leads to a fix the player can order. Diagnosability without a verb attached is still spectating; W&R never separates the two.
findings.evidence: https://www.dedoimedo.com/games/workers-resources-soviet-republic.html; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workers_&_Resources:_Soviet_Republic; docs/research/economy-mechanics.md anti-pattern list ('keep every dependency, delete every entity')

findings.title: W&R's construction system is itself the most stealable mechanic: building is production, with an autarky-vs-hard-currency fork
findings.detail: In W&R, construction is not a mana bar: construction offices dispatch your own workers and domestically produced materials (concrete, steel, prefab panels) to sites — or you pay dollars for instant foreign-built construction. That single fork (slow self-reliant vs fast hard-currency) is the Cold War planned-economy dilemma as one toggle, and it maps perfectly onto the architecture already locked: construction as a capacity pool gated by cement/steel/labor (principle #2) plus dual currency for the East (principle #9). At grand-strategy altitude this becomes a per-order choice, not per-building logistics: any development order can be Domestic (consumes the construction pool, throttled by cement/steel/labor balances) or Hard-Currency Assisted (spend scarce $/gold for imported materials and Western machinery, substantially faster). It also gives the market bloc its mirrored version — deficit-financed construction booms with debt-service consequences.
findings.evidence: https://wiki.hoodedhorse.com/Workers_Resources_Soviet_Republic/Construction; https://wiki.hoodedhorse.com/Workers_Resources_Soviet_Republic/Construction_office; docs/design/systems/economy.md (construction pool 'gated by inputs it cannot buy itself')

findings.title: The right granularity is a capped portfolio of named orders, not a build menu on 250 regions
findings.detail: The genre triangulates cleanly. HoI4's per-state queue collapsed into a solved civs-first meta (players even computed that infrastructure never pays back vs. just building factories) — placement UI without placement consequence. Victoria 3 made construction 'the #1 activity in the game' and then had to claw half of it back with an automated private queue — a queue that scales with economy size becomes a job. EU4 development is mana-clicking; Stellaris districts are fine at 10 planets and misery at 100. Terra Invicta gets the feel right by a different route: few, high-stakes, named slots, so the decision count is set by design, not by map size. Conclusion for UGS: the player holds roughly 4–8 concurrent 'development orders' (region + sector + chunky size step) plus 0–2 Great Projects, with the construction capacity pool as the natural concurrency governor. The 250 regions are where you LOOK; the portfolio is where you ACT. Adding regions to the map must never add clicks to the month.
findings.evidence: https://steamcommunity.com/app/394360/discussions/0/3307213006844285994/ (HoI4 infra-vs-factory math); Victoria 3 community: construction as '#1 activity', private construction queue debates (steamcommunity.com/app/529340 discussions); docs/research/economy-mechanics.md principle #10

findings.title: Placement is only strategic if regional endowments make sites differentially productive
findings.detail: HoI4's state placement matters only thinly (bombing range, supply); EU4's buildings barely care where they sit; and when where doesn't matter, region choice is fake agency. UGS already computes the three things that make site choice real: regional labor (rural reserves per province cohorts — principle #4, the era's binding constraint), regional power balance (surplus vs. throttled grids, already a map mode), and input adjacency (Donbas coal, Baku oil in scenario deposit data). A development order's cost/speed/output should be visibly modified by a computed 'site report': building steel capacity in a region with idle rural labor, power surplus, and coal nearby is faster and better than a greenfield. This turns geography into decisions at zero micromanagement cost, and it gives the inspector panel stakes: you read regions in order to choose between them. It also feeds pillars 1–3: capacity concentrated in one region is a bombing, invasion, and sabotage target.
findings.evidence: crates/ugs-sim/src/economy.rs (RegionalPower, region_industry by urban share, DepositKind); docs/research/economy-mechanics.md principles #4, #5; HoI4 wiki/forum consensus on infrastructure payback

findings.title: The construction layer is where the asymmetry thesis becomes visible: the planner places, the market player steers placement
findings.detail: Victoria 3's private construction queue — half of construction moved out of the player's hands and allocated by pop investment — was controversial precisely because it's the honest model of a market economy, bolted onto a game designed as a full-control builder. UGS should make that split the intended design from day one: the planned player directly authors development orders (Gosplan allocates capacity to regions — quantities), while the market player's direct builds are restricted to public goods (infrastructure, grid interconnects, Great Projects like the Interstate) and everything else is placed by autonomous firms following a simple published investment score, which the player tilts with parameters: regional tax credits, procurement contracts, interest rates. Same substrate, same region panels, opposite verbs. This is the cheapest way to pass the design doc's own first-hour test — the difference between blocs is felt in the construction screen itself, not in a policy tooltip.
findings.evidence: Victoria 3 private construction queue community debate (steamcommunity.com/app/529340); docs/design/systems/economy.md ('planner sets quantities / market sets parameters', firms' logic 'simple, published, and correct')

findings.title: Great Projects must change the graph, not stack modifiers — that's what makes ~30 of them carry a 40-year campaign
findings.detail: HoI4 national-focus buildings and EU4 monuments decay into +X% lines nobody remembers. What makes a megaproject memorable in play (and in history) is topology: Volga-Don opens a trade route, a grid interconnection merges two named grids into one balance, Virgin Lands adds arable land to a region, Aswan is an influence-war prize for whoever finances it. With the architecture's named grids, severable trade links, and regional flow balances, every Great Project can be specified as a graph edit plus an influence payout, with multi-year timelines and seeded overrun risk. They are also the correct home for drama the generic capacity pool can't carry: sabotage targets for pillar 3, prestige stakes for pillar 2, and the ceremonial announcement moments that fit the Five-Year-Plan pause cadence.
findings.evidence: docs/design/systems/economy.md (Great Projects with 'timelines, overrun risk, sabotage vulnerability, influence payouts'); genre counterexample: EU4 monuments / HoI4 focus rewards as forgettable modifier stacks

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Regional Development Orders (the core construction verb)
mechanics_recommendations.why: Converts the locked 'one decision per game-month' construction pool into placed, named, inspectable agency without per-region queues — and incrementally migrates v1's country-scalar industry into real per-region sector capacity, which is what makes regions worth inspecting at all.
mechanics_recommendations.how: State: DevelopmentOrder { region: RegionId, sector: Sector (Extraction/Steel/MachineTools/ConsumerGoods/Power/Housing), size_step: u8, points_done/points_needed, funding: Domestic|HardCurrency, priority rank }. National pool emits construction points per month = f(cement, steel, construction labor balances); points flow to orders by strict priority order (chunky ranking, no sliders). Concurrency cap ~6 (planned) / ~3 public-only (market). points_needed = base(sector, size) × site_modifier, where site_modifier is computed from regional idle labor, power surplus/deficit, and deposit adjacency, and is SHOWN as a site report before commit. Completion is a step-change: +capacity in that region's sector ledger (v1 bridge: completed orders add region-local industry on top of the urban-share distribution already computed in economy.rs). Orders complete or slots free roughly monthly — the cadence emerges from the pool, not from a timer.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Region Inspector with bottleneck verdict and linked verbs
mechanics_recommendations.why: Directly answers 'more information in regions' — and W&R teaches that diagnosability IS the fun of a planned economy, but only when every diagnosis links to a fix. Costs almost no new sim: it is mostly derivation over state that already exists (RegionalPower, cohorts, region_industry, deposits).
mechanics_recommendations.how: Per-region derived RegionLedger { labor: {employed, idle_rural_reserve, urbanization gate}, power: {capacity, demand, throttle_pct}, sectors: [(capacity, utilization_pct, limiting_factor)], flows in/out, verdict: Bottleneck enum (Power|Labor|Inputs|Transport|Demand|None) }. UI: click region → dossier headed by one verdict sentence ('Donbas: coal output power-throttled to 71%'), each line a hyperlink to the verb that addresses it (power deficit → 'order power plant here' pre-fills a DevelopmentOrder; labor shortage → housing order / urbanization policy). Add bottleneck and per-commodity map modes beside the existing power mode. Planned-bloc twist per the falsified-reports principle: the ledger shows REPORTED figures; audit actions reveal true ones.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Dual-track order funding: Domestic vs Hard-Currency Assist (the W&R steal)
mechanics_recommendations.why: W&R's construction-office-vs-dollars fork is the planned-economy dilemma in one toggle, and it lands on mechanics already locked (construction gated by non-purchasable inputs; dual currency for the East). It also keeps the pool strategic: when cement/steel are the binding constraint, hard currency is the only way to jump the queue — at the cost of the resource that also buys Western tech and grain.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Per order, funding: Domestic consumes cement+steel+construction labor from national balances (order stalls visibly when they run dry — the stall reason shows in the inspector); HardCurrencyAssist spends $ per point (imported materials/machinery) for +50–100% point rate and immunity to domestic material shortages. Market bloc mirror: Budget (taxes) vs Debt-financed (bond issue, interest burden, inflation pressure). Tuning values in a tuning module per convention. This single enum makes Soviet gold/oil exports, Western credit lines, and COCOM embargoes all bite the construction screen.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Great Projects as authored graph edits with overrun risk
mechanics_recommendations.why: The generic pool carries volume; ~30 named projects carry the campaign's memory and the cross-pillar drama (prestige, sabotage, influence payouts). They must be topological — a modifier stack would make them forgettable and re-import mudflation.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Hand-authored RON list (historian-sourced): { id, name, host_region(s), points_needed (large), prerequisite techs/resources, effect: GraphEdit (NewTradeLink | MergeGrids | AddArable | AddCapacity{region, sector} | UnlockPort...), influence_payout, overrun: monthly SimRng-forked roll adding points while unfinished, sabotage_surface for pillar 3 }. One dedicated project slot beside the order slots; starting/completing one is a ceremonial paused moment with a dated announcement. Seed list: Volga-Don Canal, Virgin Lands, Great Volga hydro cascade, Aswan (contested financing), US Interstate Highways, St. Lawrence Seaway, national grid interconnections.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Market-side private placement: firms build, the player tilts the score
mechanics_recommendations.why: Without this, the market bloc's construction screen is just planning with extra steps and the pillar's first-hour test fails. Victoria 3's private queue proves players accept firms building autonomously when the logic is legible and steerable.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Monthly, a private construction point pool (scaled by GDP, interest rate) is allocated across regions/sectors by a published score: expected_return = regional demand gap × price − wages − taxes + subsidies − power_throttle_penalty. Player instruments (parameters only): regional tax credit (costs budget), procurement contract (government commits to buy N units of military/machine output at fixed price for Y years — summons capacity where FIRMS choose, often not where the player hoped: pork-barrel realism), interest rate (already implemented) scaling the pool. Player direct-builds limited to infrastructure, grids, and Great Projects. The region inspector shows the score per region so steering is a legible game, not a black box.

pitfalls: Decision count scaling with map size. The moment inspecting 250 regions turns into acting on 250 regions, you've rebuilt Victoria 3's 'construction is the #1 activity' problem. The order-slot cap is the firewall — resist every future feature that adds a per-region button, and test the cadence: a full play-month at speed 3 should present at most one or two construction choices.

A solved opening build order (HoI4's civs-first disease). If one sequence is always right, the portfolio is fake. Defenses already in the architecture — the binding constraint must migrate (cement → power → labor across a campaign), site modifiers make the best next order depend on the map, and rural labor exhaustion imposes diminishing returns per region. Playtest question: 'what do you build first?' should have no single correct answer across starts.

Information without verbs — shipping the region inspector before the development orders. That makes regions MORE visible as a simulation the player still can't touch, which worsens the exact complaint. Ship the verb and the ledger together; every diagnosis line links to an action or states why none exists.

The market interface collapsing into planning-with-extra-steps. If procurement contracts and subsidies let the market player deterministically place a factory in a chosen region, the asymmetry thesis dies. Firms must retain the location choice; the player buys probability and quantity, not coordinates.

Migration risk regionalizing v1's country-scalar industry: the urban-share distribution in economy.rs currently recomputes each tick from the scalar, so per-region deltas from completed orders must layer on top deterministically (BTreeMap ordering, no HashMap iteration) and survive save/load via the command log. Do the bridge as scalar-distribution + region-local additive capacity first; fully regional sector chains can come later without breaking saves.
analysts.first_hour_test: Boot as the USSR, January 1950, open the economy. SEE: the map in a new development mode — ~30 Soviet economic regions shaded by industrial capacity, with bottleneck glyphs (a power icon pulsing on the Donbas, a labor icon on Central Asia). Click the Urals: a dossier with one verdict line ('Urals: machine-tool output limited by electricity, grid at 84%'), a small ledger (labor: 1.2M idle rural reserve; power: deficit; coal: adjacent; steel: exporting to Center region), and a site report grading it for each sector. Beside the map, the Plan Board: the construction pool's monthly output, six order slots — four pre-filled by the 1950 scenario (historically sourced reconstruction orders), two EMPTY, and the Volga-Don Canal sitting in the Great Project slot at 31% with an overrun warning. FIRST DECISION: fill an empty slot — the inspector has already framed the choice as a real dilemma with no dominant answer: a coal-power station in the Urals (fixes the verdict you just read, Domestic funding, 14 months), expanded steel in Donbas (faster, but power-throttled until someone fixes THAT), or housing in Moscow to open the urbanization gate. Toggle the funding: Domestic says '14 months, stalls if cement runs short'; Hard-Currency Assist says '9 months, costs $120M of the $340M reserve earmarked for machine-tool imports.' Commit, unpause, and within a play-month the order's progress bar ticks on the region itself and the Donbas verdict line updates. It feels like playing rather than watching because every piece of information you were shown existed to set up a choice you then made, the choice was placed on a named piece of the map you can revisit, and its consequence (the throttle number moving) is legible in the same panel that provoked it. The USA mirror makes the pillar felt immediately: the same region dossiers, but the Plan Board is replaced by an Investment Climate board — private firms are already building (a queue you watch but don't own), and your empty slots are two public-works slots plus parameter dials; your first decision is a procurement contract or a tax credit, and the firms answer it next month — somewhere of THEIR choosing.

principles.principle: 1. No panel without a verb — information and action ship in the same slice, or the 'watching a simulation' complaint gets worse, not better. Every dossier row must terminate in a button, a deep-link to the screen holding the relevant verb, or a one-line inline 'why'.
principles.support: victoria3-agency (finding 6, pitfall 3), construction-agency (pitfall 3: 'shipping the inspector before the development orders worsens the exact complaint'), ui-information-design (verb-anchored readout rule, enforced as an acceptance test), asymmetric-agency (pitfall 6: ship ledger cards first but never alone), systems-integration (map mode answers 'where', dossier 'why', project menu 'what can I do').

principles.principle: 2. The unit of regional legibility is the computed binding constraint, not the flow table. The sim already computes which factor limits each region's output; print the argmin as a one-word status and a one-sentence verdict ('URALS OUTPUT LIMITED BY POWER: GENERATION COVERS 82% OF DEMAND'). At 250 regions this converts a data lake into a triage list.
principles.support: victoria3-agency (Vic3 makes you infer the bottleneck; UGS should state it), construction-agency (W&R's magic is diagnosability — one verdict line per region), ui-information-design (Cities: Skylines paint-only-the-bottleneck principle; the shipped battle-inspector diagnosis sentence as in-codebase precedent), systems-integration (bottleneck classification from existing ratios).

principles.principle: 3. Decision count is a designed budget (~2–4 meaningful economy decisions per game-month), fixed by slot caps — it must never scale with region count. principles.support: All seven. victoria3-agency (Vic3's 50-state whack-a-mole × 5 warning), construction-agency (4–8 order portfolio; Terra Invicta's designed slot count), cold-war-economic-historian (the Politburo made ~a dozen priority calls per plan), asymmetric-agency (explicit 2–4/month budget for both blocs), projects-as-agency (2–4 concurrent projects = one event per month), ui-information-design (triage-list cognition), systems-integration (hard caps as 'the design, not a tuning afterthought').

principles.principle: 4. The core verb is placing named projects on regions, priced as standing flows against the shared construction pool (which remains gated by materials it cannot buy), so most delays are emergent and attributable — and completions are step-changes the substrate models (MW on a named grid, capacity in a region's ledger, a graph edit), never '+5%' modifiers.
principles.support: construction-agency (development orders + Great Projects as graph edits), projects-as-agency (flow-denominated commitment; unattributed overruns are noise; payload-inflation pitfall), victoria3-agency (the universal build verb, throttled to monthly cadence), systems-integration (redirect invest_out through a pool into slots; four project kinds land on existing consumers), cold-war-economic-historian (campaigns as named regional gambles with multi-year ramps).

principles.principle: 5. The asymmetry must live in the decision stream, not the lever list: the planner initiates and commands quantities in named places; the market player never places industry — they authorize public goods and tilt a PUBLISHED, deterministic investment allocator with zones/contracts/rates, and firms keep the location choice. The market side only works if the response is legible and attributed ('where capital went and why'); otherwise it is Vic3's despised private queue.
principles.support: All seven. victoria3-agency (re-centralizing mods as the tombstone of 'same game minus control'), construction-agency (firms build, player tilts the score; player buys probability, not coordinates), cold-war-economic-historian (US agency = acts, amortization certificates, procurement geography — never quantities), asymmetric-agency (planner authors, market player referees; contracts fix price and ceiling only), projects-as-agency (authorize + fund vs. command), systems-integration (wrong-interface command rejection already exists as the enforcement pattern), ui-information-design (asymmetric chrome is load-bearing).

principles.principle: 6. Epistemic texture is the pillar's signature UI feature: the planner's regional figures are REPORTED (lies must be discoverable via audits and honest tells like queues/black-market indices, never silent wrongness), the market player's figures are true but lagged ('SURVEY, Q4 1949'), foreign regions render through espionage fidelity at 2 significant figures — and the sim never fabricates quantities the inspector cannot account for.
principles.support: victoria3-agency (ex-nihilo goods destroy trust; the one licensed lie must be a discoverable mechanic), ui-information-design (PLAN/REPORTED columns, lagged survey stamps, war-legibility fuzz rules transfer verbatim), asymmetric-agency (misreporting without tells reads as a bug — Kremlingames reception), cold-war-economic-historian (Ryazan 1959 fraud; petition/report texture), projects-as-agency (Falsify verb with separate true/reported tracks), systems-integration (pitfall: new surfaces must not leak truth past the misreporting and espionage systems).

principles.principle: 7. Economic display is monthly, date-stamped, and still between boundaries, with a curated heartbeat: 3–6 severity-ranked wire lines per month, each carrying a RegionId and a cause, plus an optional briefing card at rollover. Wiggling per-tick numbers ARE the 'watching a simulation' feeling rendered in UI; unattributed events are noise.
principles.support: ui-information-design (negative-space finding: AS-OF stamps, no jitter), victoria3-agency (inbox capped at 3–5 items, severity-ranked), asymmetric-agency (event-driven cadence, pause-friendly), projects-as-agency (every delay arrives with its cause attached or should not happen), cold-war-economic-historian (2–4 prioritized regional notices monthly).

principles.principle: 8. Build by thawing what exists, not rebuilding: promote the init-frozen region_industry to dynamic serialized state, redirect part of the existing invest_out through the pool, and let surplus auto-invest exactly as today — so all 226 AI countries and passive players keep current behavior with zero new AI code, and the military-command layer's proven shape (player decides what/where, sim executes) is copied directly.
principles.support: systems-integration (the central finding: substrate exists but is frozen; the military layer as template; 85% of the dossier is presentation over existing state), construction-agency (bridge migration: scalar distribution + region-local additive capacity first, deterministic BTreeMap layering).

principles.principle: 9. Placement is only a decision if sites differ and offers are situational: regional endowments (idle labor, power surplus/deficit, deposits) must visibly modify project cost/speed/effect, and Great Project offers must be predicates over sim state, not an era menu — otherwise region choice is fake agency and the catalog focus-tree-ifies into a solved opening.
principles.support: construction-agency (site reports; HoI4's civs-first solved meta as the anti-pattern), projects-as-agency (condition-gated Offer Board; 'do two campaigns produce different ledgers by 1955?' playtest check), systems-integration (power-factor feedback already wired, just has constant inputs), cold-war-economic-historian (offers arise from real region state — grain shortfall gates Virgin Lands).

synthesis.shape:
The v1 slice is one loop — see a place, read its constraint, commit a project, watch the consequence ramp — built almost entirely by thawing state the sim already computes, plus one new verb family. It has four layers.

**Sim substrate (the thaw).** Promote `region_industry` from init-frozen distribution to a serialized `RegionalIndustry { by_region: BTreeMap<RegionId, u64> }` resource, seeded from the existing urban-share split, folded into the determinism digest; country industry becomes the derived sum (kept as a cache for dashboards, misreporting, and intel). `update_production` computes output per-region using each region's own power factor (RegionalPower already computes it) times the national materials ratio, so a throttled grid now hurts the specific region and the feedback loop that is already wired gets moving inputs. Add two cheap init-time aggregates: `region_deposits` and per-region cohort sums. Then a monthly `RegionSnapshot` per region, recomputed on `new_month` in TickSet::Economy after balances: population + trend, power gen/demand/factor, industry (actual and reported), grain ratio, deposits, and a `ConstraintKind` = argmin over normalized limiters (power factor, labor ratio, input ratio) with a severity band. Integer math, BTreeMap iteration, digest-tested. This snapshot is the single source for everything the player sees; nothing in the UI reads per-tick sim state.

**Legibility layer (three surfaces, one ladder).** (1) A **BOTTLENECK map mode** beside the existing power mode: categorical color by ConstraintKind, three chunky severity bands, legend rows showing national counts ('POWER-LIMITED: 14 REGIONS') that click-filter the ledger. Planned countries additionally get a plan-fulfillment tint mode (reported figures); market countries an economic-climate mode (true, lagged). (2) A **National Economy Ledger** in the econ panel: one sortable row per region — NAME | POP | INDUSTRY | PWR% | FOOD% | CONSTRAINT | trend glyph — with bloc-specific extra columns (planner: PLAN/REPORTED; market: TAX BASE/GROWTH, lagged a quarter). Sorting is the decision aid; click-through opens the dossier. (3) The **Region Dossier**: a fixed one-page teletype document, the economic sibling of the shipped battle inspector. Header (name, owner, pop + trend, character line like 'COAL / HEAVY INDUSTRY'), four flat blocks (PEOPLE, POWER with a gen-vs-demand bar, PRODUCTION with deposit pips and named complexes, FOOD), active project card with progress and 'slowed by' cause, and a footer that prints the binding-constraint verdict sentence plus 2–3 verb buttons. All figures stamped 'AS OF 1 JAN 1950' and still between months. Planner self-view shows REPORTED figures (v1: the existing national padding factor applied proportionally — no new drift state yet); market self-view shows true figures with survey-lag stamps; foreign regions render the same form through the espionage penetration model at 2 significant figures, unknown blocks printed 'NO COVERAGE'. No nested tooltips anywhere; causes print inline.

**The verb (construction pool + project slots).** A `Construction` resource: per-country pool accruing `invest_out × ~500‰` monthly (the other half auto-converts exactly as today — the AI-default and passive-player guardrail), draining into active projects. Slots: 2 generic + 1 Great Project. `ProjectKind { IndustrialExpansion, PowerStation, AgriMechanization, Great(id) }` — each lands on an existing consumer: +RegionalIndustry (which also raises regional power demand — a real tradeoff), +built_power into the region's capacity formula, +yield_permille, and Great payloads as step-changes/graph edits plus a wire ceremony and influence payout. Project intake each month is scaled by the host region's power factor and the national materials ratio — the cannot-buy-itself gate — so a project in a browned-out region visibly slows, and the dossier names why. Commands through the queue: `StartProject { country, region, kind }` (validated: owned AND held, slot free, kind legal for the country's economic system — reusing the wrong-interface rejection pattern) and `CancelProject`. Site differentiation v1: a small site report on the start dialog (idle labor, power surplus, deposit adjacency modify cost/time), so choosing WHERE is a decision. Great Projects ship as a hand-authored, historian-sourced RON catalog of ~8 entries with condition-gated offers (Volga-Don Canal ACTIVE at start — the player inherits a real 1950 project; Kuibyshev HPP offerable because the Middle Volga grid is deficit; Turkmen Canal as the priced trap; US: St. Lawrence Seaway, Interstate 1956, Paducah diffusion plant). Overruns in v1 are emergent only (satisfied-fraction of committed flows), with one stochastic event class reserved for Great Projects, forked `rng.fork(b"projects")` by project id, always attributed in the wire.

**Asymmetric interfaces over the same machinery.** Planned countries: StartProject accepts all kinds; starts and completions print ceremonial wire decrees; the map lies to them per the reported figures. Market countries: StartProject accepts only PowerStation/Great (public works); their regional verb is `SetDevelopmentZone { region }` (cap 3), and every month a deterministic private-investment pass distributes `invest_out × PRIVATE_SHARE` across regions by a published integer formula — f(power factor, urban labor, zone bonus, tax level) — adding directly to RegionalIndustry. The dossier attributes it: 'PRIVATE INVESTMENT THIS MONTH: +0.4 (power surplus, zone active)'. The monthly briefing gives the market player a 'where capital went and why' digest; parameter play is steering a river, visibly.

**Heartbeat.** On `new_month`, 3–6 severity-ranked wire lines from snapshot deltas crossing thresholds (grid deficit onset, constraint change, project slowed/completed, food ratio dip), each with a RegionId click-through; optional auto-pause briefing card at rollover with top changes, worst regions, and one templated recommendation derived only from visible constraint data — so the player can learn to beat it.

Nothing here rebuilds the sim: quotas, market levers, commodity balances, agriculture, and grids all stay national or already-regional as they are. The slice thaws one resource, adds one resource, one command family, one snapshot, and three UI surfaces — and the locked architecture's regional industry chain, priority lists, and audit game all have their landing zones prepared rather than preempted.

tensions.tension: What is the planned player's CORE verb: project placement (construction-agency, projects-as-agency, systems-integration) or priority designation — scarce flags/ranked lists deciding who eats shortage first (cold-war-economic-historian, asymmetric-agency, victoria3-agency's priority lists)?
tensions.recommendation: Projects in v1, priority in v1.1 — sequencing, not either/or. Projects land on consumers that exist today (military_stock, grids, agriculture) and reuse the military-command template; priority resolution needs an incidence order over commodity balances that is worth building once regional flow detail exists to allocate. Both analysts' histories agree the real Soviet game was BOTH (build the combine AND rank who starves); ship the buildable half first, and design the dossier's PLAN block so a priority rank column can slot in without layout change.

tensions.tension: Who initiates the monthly decision: the sim drafts 3–5 scored proposals and the player disposes (victoria3-agency's construction council — Gosplan proposes), or the player diagnoses from the dossier and initiates (construction-agency, systems-integration)?
tensions.recommendation: Player-initiated in v1, with the briefing card's single templated recommendation as the thin end of the proposal wedge. The acid-test moment everyone wants is the player choosing the power station BECAUSE THEY SAW the bottleneck — a proposal menu risks reducing that to a rubber stamp before the diagnosis loop is proven fun. Revisit a full proposal engine when playtests show players ignoring the map; the recommendation line already exercises the scoring logic it would need.

tensions.tension: Overrun model: primarily emergent from flow shortfalls (projects-as-agency, systems-integration) vs. genuinely stochastic gambles — Virgin Lands must be able to fail (cold-war-economic-historian: 'do not make campaigns deterministic buttons').
tensions.recommendation: Both, partitioned by tier. Generic projects: purely emergent (satisfied_fraction of committed flows) — a delay is always attributable to a named shortage. Great Projects/campaigns additionally roll seeded events (rng forked by project id) for geology, weather, sabotage — always attributed in the wire once discovered. The historian is right that a known payoff curve is a purchase, but that argument only bears on the big named gambles; making a routine power station stochastic would just read as dice.

tensions.tension: How much epistemic machinery in v1: per-region reported-vs-actual drift, audit verb, and diegetic tells (asymmetric-agency, ui-information-design call the columns load-bearing) vs. presentation-only padding now, full audit game later (systems-integration).
tensions.recommendation: Middle path: v1 shows PLAN/REPORTED columns by distributing the EXISTING national padding proportionally (no new sim state, no truth leak, the player learns in minute ten their dashboard can lie), and the AUDIT button ships greyed with a tooltip naming the coming mechanic — or not at all. Per-region drift, the audit command, and queue/black-market tells are the first fast-follow, because asymmetric-agency's warning stands: a lie without tells reads as a bug, and building tells properly is its own slice.

tensions.tension: Market first-hour texture: an inbox of contract bids from named competing complexes (asymmetric-agency's Contract Book, construction-agency's procurement contracts) vs. zones + published allocator + attributed digest only (systems-integration).
tensions.recommendation: Zones + digest in v1; the Contract Book is the first market-side follow-up, wired to the existing procurement lever. The digest already gives the market player something to read and a cause-and-effect loop to steer; contract bids need named complexes with bidding AI and deterministic proposal generation — real work that shouldn't gate the slice. But schedule it: the decision-budget parity warning (everyone plays USA if planned is 6 clicks and market is 1 — or vice versa, nobody plays USA if market months are silent) is a genuine balance risk the digest alone may not cover.

tensions.tension: Scope of the historical apparatus: sovnarkhoz-vs-ministerial administrative structure (historian), Domestic-vs-Hard-Currency funding fork (construction-agency), and contested foreign bids/Aswan (historian, projects-as-agency) are each pitched as near-core.
tensions.recommendation: All three deferred, explicitly and in this order of return: contested foreign bids first (fuses pillars 2–4 and reuses the project machinery wholesale — the best post-v1 payoff), hard-currency funding second (needs the dual-currency system the locked architecture promises but the sim lacks), sovnarkhoz reform last (a superb v2 strategic layer, but it modifies systems — priority flags, inter-region flows — that don't exist yet). None of these are disagreements about the v1 shape; they are competing claims on the sequel slices, and writing the order down now prevents scope creep into v1.

synthesis.first_hour_acid_test:
A new player boots as the USSR, January 1st 1950, and presses E. They do not see a country scalar — they see the Ledger: fifteen named regions (MOSCOW, DONBASS, URALS, KUZBASS, BAKU...), each with population, industry, PWR%, FOOD%, a one-word constraint tag, and a trend glyph. Two rows carry an amber POWER-LIMITED tag, and the PLAN and REPORTED columns sit side by side — the first quiet hint that this dashboard is somebody's word, not ground truth. One keystroke flips the map to BOTTLENECK mode: the same two regions glow amber. The numbers have places.

They click URALS. A one-page teletype dossier: 'AS OF 1 JAN 1950 — POP 13.9M ▲ — COAL / HEAVY INDUSTRY', deposit pips, an employment ramp on a named complex, a generation-vs-demand bar visibly short, and the footer verdict: 'OUTPUT LIMITED BY POWER: GENERATION COVERS 82% OF DEMAND', with a START PROJECT button beside it. Below, the CONSTRUCTION section shows the pool accruing from the 45% investment quota, 1 of 2 generic slots free — and the Great Project slot already occupied by the Volga-Don Canal at 61%, inherited, drawing cement from the Lower Volga, its pin on the map wearing a progress ring. The player owns a portfolio before they have made a move.

The first decision writes itself from what the map showed, and it is a real dilemma: a power station in the Urals (fixes the verdict they just read, 8 months, site report notes coal adjacency), or an industrial expansion in fully-powered Kuzbass (more output now, but it raises Kuzbass power demand — the site report says so). They start the Urals station; the wire prints 'COUNCIL OF MINISTERS DECREES URALS POWER PROGRAM'. They unpause. At the February rollover the briefing card pauses the game: 'URALS POWER PROGRAM 12% — ON SCHEDULE. KUZBASS GRID DEFICIT ONSET — INDUSTRY THROTTLED 8%. RECOMMEND: CONSTRUCTION TO KUZBASS (POWER).' The player can take the recommendation or beat it — the data it derives from is all on their screen. In month three the wire reports the Volga-Don's cement delivery at 74%, attributed to a Donbass shortfall, and the project card offers the choice the whole loop has been teaching them to make: accept the delay, or reallocate. By the Korean War in June, the player has a portfolio they authored, regions they know by name and ailment, and a map that answers back monthly — inspect place, read constraint, commit the scarce increment, get graded by next month's document. That is playing.

The USA proves the asymmetry in one contrast. Same E key, same dossier form — but every figure is stamped 'SURVEY, Q4 1949', honest and late, and the URALS-equivalent click on the Tennessee Valley region shows 'PRIVATE INVESTMENT THIS MONTH: +0.4 (power surplus, urban labor)' with no START PROJECT button for industry at all. The player's verbs are a development zone on the throttled region, the interest rate, and a public-works slot (the Seaway sits on the offer board, pending authorization); next month's digest shows where private capital actually went and why — sometimes not where they hoped. The Soviet player commanded a place; the American player tilted a field and watched it answer. Same substrate, same page, opposite hands.
